decompositions.name: Fast flag raid (strike group reaches our flags soon after the dam opens and carries them off while losing or tying on kills)

prerequisites.why: When opponents do this, the strike group is mostly their main army standing on our side of the map. Repeated grabs after a carrier dies need bodies near the flag for a long time. Our own raid volume rises with this metric.
prerequisites.evidence: Robots in the enemy half at r250 (inEnemy250): 10 vs 24 against the 15 bots that beat us (444 games). In our 96 losses by CAPTURE before r600 (of 414 census losses) it is 6 vs 25.5, and they make 14 pickups to our 1 while kills are even at 71-71 (we out-kill them in 49 of the 96). It flips to 18 vs 13 in our wins. Per game it correlates with our pickups (rho 0.35, about +0.38 at r300). By tercile of our inEnemy250, our pickups are 1/4/6 and our captures 0.45/0.66/0.79 per game, but our win rate stays at 15/14/18%. firstEnemySide is 202 vs 202, so the first crossing is at par and the shortfall is in numbers.

prerequisites.why: A pickup only pays if the carrier gets home. Pickups made by raiders deep in the enemy half, away from our army, die before converting.
prerequisites.evidence: Pooled over 444 games vs the 15: our carriers die 0.87 times per pickup vs 0.66 for theirs (0.80 vs 0.69 against the other opponents). Carrier rounds per pickup are 24.5 vs 17.7. In the code, carryFlag() just calls Nav.moveTo toward the nearest spawn tile with no threat term. Allies escort only when no enemy is visible (Duck.fieldTarget). Micro.fight pulls only toward ENEMY carriers. C.RELAY=false. On the 30 field cells vs the 15, captures per pickup fell from 0.17 (g_iter1 control) to 0.11 (arch_rush10) and 0.04 (arch_rush).

prerequisites.why: A raid that is not simply the army needs a real group: a shared target, a rendezvous and an arrival together, so raiders do not arrive one at a time and get killed.
prerequisites.evidence: No census metric exists. In the code, the arch_rush10 squad is creation indices 3..12 (Duck.isRusher). Each rusher picks its own target from its own position (fieldTargetFrom(G.me), or flankTarget with RUSH_FLANK). They start from wherever they gathered at the dam and never regroup. There is no squad slot in Comms. Cohesion forcing hurt (gr4 20-23, gr8 4-18). The flank squad fl10 went 20-23 over two band seeds.

prerequisites.why: Bodies sent on a raid are taken off the home front, so our flags must hold without them. Otherwise the raid trades our flags for theirs.
prerequisites.evidence: They pick up our flags 17 times a game vs our 4 (median). 96 of our 414 census losses are captures before r600, and 31 come before r400. On the 30 cells vs the 15, their captures rose from 67 (control) to 72 (arch_rush10) and 78 (arch_rush). Every body-based or trap defence was rejected: 2 defenders 9-25, alert x4 12-31, fortress 16-29, flag-tile stun 19-23 on the band. We kill 11 of their carriers a game and still lose the flags.

prerequisites.why: A fast raid needs to know where the flags are when the dam drops. Opponents that relocate flags (T2) lengthen the search.
prerequisites.evidence: First enemy-flag sighting (firstFlagSight): r271 vs r232 against the 15 (n=426), and r243 vs r222 in the fast losses. It is at par against bots we beat (228.5 vs 231.5). It is not the binding limit: per game it does not correlate with our pickups (rho -0.05), and committing bodies moved our first pickup on the top-bot cells from r359 (control) to r282 (arch_rush10) and r258 (arch_rush). In the code, the army walks to the nearest broadcast hint, which can be up to dist 10 from the flag while vision reaches about 4.5. Ducks then idle on the hint with no search. Sym.observe is never called, so symmetry comes only from the r1-3 broadcasts.

prerequisites.why: Picking up, carrying and capturing are the core actions of the raid.
prerequisites.evidence: carrierSpeed is 0.47 vs 0.45. Pooled captures per pickup vs the 15 are 0.115 for us and 0.106 for them; the median of per-game ratios (0.06 vs 0.13) is pulled down by our games with few pickups. Our first pickup median is r248 across the survey, which tags us as already doing 'fast raid'. Relay code exists (a2relay 81/110 vs control 84/110). The 4 vs 17 pickup gap is a volume problem that belongs to C11/C12, not a pickup or carry mechanics problem.

prerequisites.why: Raiders must survive contact long enough to grab and re-grab the flag. The tactic works for opponents even when they lose on kills.
prerequisites.evidence: Kills vs deaths are 212 vs 220 in our losses and 71 vs 71 in the 96 fast losses (we out-kill them in 49). The census line vs the 15 is 246 vs 292. The rush micro (RUSH_THREAT_COST 150, which pushes through threats) was never measured on its own. The smooth-scoring micro MICRO_V2 was rejected 1-25.

prerequisites.why: The raiders and the carrier have to cover the map efficiently.
prerequisites.evidence: firstEnemySide is 202 vs 202 and carrierSpeed 0.47 vs 0.45. Our own ABA is 9.4% and still% is 32.6%; there are no opponent navstats to compare, so the evidence is partial.

prerequisites.why: Stun traps freeze defenders and chasers while raiders grab and carry. Strong bots raid while out-trapping us.
prerequisites.evidence: trapsBuilt 187.5 vs 239 vs the 15, and 66 vs 93 in the fast losses. Across 35 opponents that pick up our flags, their stun traps by r400 (stun400) correlate with our loss rate at rho 0.68. Combat stun traps are our only load-bearing trap habit (ablation 16-26). Rushers never build traps: Duck.turn() returns into rush() before placeCombatTrap().

prerequisites.why: A bank funds the fight-time stun traps that let a push hold ground.
prerequisites.evidence: gathered400 is 3900 vs 4950, and our bank at r250 is about 250 vs 1910 (survey, g_iter1 vs the 15). Per game it does not correlate with our pickups (rho 0.01). The bank arms c5bank and c6pair were both neutral at 82/110.

prerequisites.why: Respawns that flow toward the raid or our own carrier keep up the grab volume and the escort.
prerequisites.evidence: meanAlive is 44.9 vs 44.6. In the code, trySpawn targets an enemy-carrier intercept, then an alerted home flag, then the field target. Nothing respawns toward our own carrier or a squad.

prerequisites.why: A coordinated squad needs a shared target and rendezvous slot, and escorts need fresh positions of our own carriers.
prerequisites.evidence: No metric exists, only code inspection. The shared array holds the enemy flag registry (slots 1-9), carrier sightings of our flags (13-19), alerts and homes. There is no squad target or rendezvous slot and no broadcast of our own carrier's position.

prerequisites.why: Staging the strike group during setup and building no setup traps (banking instead) let top bots hit right at r200. hsmalladi's instance also bundles flag relocation, digging, a bank and the relay.
prerequisites.evidence: Our army gathers at the dam from r150 and traps the dam front; removing those traps was about neutral (ab1nodam 20-16). Nothing stages a squad. Of the 15, 6 move their flags in setup. hsmalladi has flagMoveDist 39, 60 digs, a bank of 1288, water traps and the relay.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
The copy added only the elementary layer of T1, getting bodies onto an enemy flag soon after r200, and we largely had that layer already. Our first pickup is r248 (survey median), and the survey already counts us as a fast raider. Speed is also not what separates strong bots from weak ones. Among the 35 opponents that pick up our flags in at least half their games, the round of their first pickup has rank correlation +0.10 with our loss rate. The 16 fastest of them (first pickup at r260 or earlier) beat us less often: mean loss rate 0.37 against 0.49 for the slower ones. Volume (pickups, rho 0.55), stun traps (0.68) and captures (0.96) are what track our losses.

On the 30 field cells against the 15 bots that beat us, the copy did what it was built to do:
- **Faster reach:** our first pickup moved from r359 (g_iter1 control) to r282 (arch_rush10) and r258 (arch_rush).
- **More pickups:** non-relay pickups rose from 141 to 168 and 332.
- **Fewer captures:** ours fell from 24 to 18 and 13, which is 0.17, 0.11 and 0.04 captures per pickup.
- **More enemy captures:** theirs rose from 67 to 72 and 78.

Isolated raiders grabbed flags deep in the enemy half and died carrying them, because carrier protection (C9) is missing. The bodies also came out of the army and the home front, and C11 and C10 were already below par.

The opponents' version is mostly carried by their army rather than a detached squad. In our 96 losses by capture before r600, kills are even at 71-71, but they have 25.5 robots in our half at r250 to our 6 and make 14 pickups to our 1. T1 is the visible end of winning the territory clash after the dam opens, combined with volume re-grabs. In hsmalladi it comes bundled with T2, T3, T4, T5 and T7.

Was the test itself adequate?
- **All-out rush:** the verdict is sound. It went 0 gained and 22 lost on paired cells and 5/32 head to head.
- **10-duck squad:** the verdict is weak. It was a full-field block with only 30 cells against the 15 that beat us (4-4 there, 3-3 elsewhere), so it could only resolve about ±5 games of 110. The flank variant fl10 went 20-23 over 240 band games.
- **Not a faithful copy:** the rushers are creation indices 3..12 that each pick their own target from wherever they gathered. They never regroup, never place combat traps (rush() returns before placeCombatTrap), and their carriers walk straight to the nearest spawn tile.
- **Wrong gate:** no capability readout (pickups, captures per pickup, inEnemy250, their captures) was used to decide. The numbers above were recovered afterwards from survey.csv.

A guess, not confirmed: our deficit in robots in the enemy half comes from the kite/hold micro giving up ground in the r200-r250 clash, and from spending the bank on setup traps instead of fight stuns. The aggression and bank arms were neutral, so this is unproven.
buildOrder: C11 (territory/tempo), with its parts C5 (combat stun traps while pushing, which rushers currently skip) and C3 (a bank to pay for them): raise robots in the enemy half at r250 against the band from about 10 toward 18, the level in our wins, while keeping kills even. Gate arms on inEnemy250 first: across 240 games two arms differ detectably at about 1.7 robots, while the same block only resolves about ±16 wins.

C10 (hold the home flags with fewer bodies, using standing defences rather than guards): needed before any squad is diverted. On the 30 copy cells their captures rose from 67 to 72 and 78 when bodies left; they currently pick up our flags 17 times a game.

C9 (carrier protection): escorts in combat, a carrier route that avoids threats, and a relay to the escorts. Target: carrier deaths per pickup at or below 0.66, and captures per pickup holding at the control's 0.17 as pickups rise.

C12 together with C7 (a real strike group): a shared target and rendezvous slot, raiders arriving together, raiders that keep placing combat traps, and respawns that reinforce the squad or our carrier.

C1 (flag localisation): search around the broadcast hint instead of idling on it, and infer symmetry from terrain (Sym.observe is never called). Target: first enemy-flag sighting vs the 15 at r235 or earlier instead of r271.
Then retry T1, preferably as a squad on top of the raised C11, and first check whether it already shows up as army-borne pickups once C11 is at par, as it does in our wins.

decompositions.name: Flags relocated in setup (edges/corners far from spawn, often behind water)

prerequisites.why: The act itself: pick legal spots at least 6 apart, carry each flag there in setup with the +20 carry cooldown, and drop it before r200 so it becomes the start location (RULES: flags closer than dist2 36 at r200 all reset to spawn).
prerequisites.evidence: Distance only. a2reloc moved flags in 108 of 110 games (2 with flagMoveDist 0). Median flagMoveDist was 26, a sum over the 3 flags of about 9 tiles each. The 6 movers that beat us have medians of 13, 17, 17.5, 21, 37.5 and 39 (hsmalladi), so their median is about 19. Shipped src/bot has C.RELOCATE_FLAGS=false, so g_iter1's flagMoveDist is 0. Placement quality is below par: see the terrain item.

prerequisites.why: The tactic as observed puts flags behind water and on map edges. That needs a stored wall/water grid and land-path distance from the enemy, not straight-line distance. The broadcast hint (within dist2 100 of a dropped flag) shows raiders where the flag is anyway, so only a longer real path slows them. Calling this required is partly a guess (no replay trace of hsmalladi's paths).
prerequisites.evidence: G.java keeps no map arrays and Nav.java is memoryless bug nav. Duck.relocTarget scores grid points by dist2 to the enemy centroid minus half the dist2 to our spawn, with no terrain term. It searches only x,y from 2 to W-3, so edge spots like hsmalladi's (22,0), (30,0) and (30,8) can never be chosen. Sym.observe is defined and never called (no call site in src/bot). Effect: on cells against the 15 that beat us, the opponent's median first pickup was 269 with relocation vs 268.5 without (n=68 each): plain relocation did not slow their first raid.

prerequisites.why: Relocation only buys time. The time is worth something only if we capture enemy flags during it (a flag race). If we cannot, a delayed loss is still a loss.
prerequisites.evidence: Census, vs the 15 bots that beat us: pickups 4 vs 17, captured 0 vs 3, capture rate 0.06 vs 0.13 (carrier speed 0.47 vs 0.45 is at par). a2reloc, 30 cells vs those bots: our pickups rose (median 3.5 to 6.5, higher in 21 of 30 cells) but our captures stayed at median 0 (fewer in 9 cells, more in 7). In the 8 control losses by CAPTURE before r700, the relocated twins survived 85 to 1600 rounds longer but we captured only 0 to 2 flags in each.

prerequisites.why: The extra time pays off only if the army is pushing into the enemy half and reaching their flags while ours are hard to reach.
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the 15 that beat us: robots in the enemy half at r250, us 10 vs them 24 (r300: 10 vs 22). In our wins this flips to 18 vs 13. First enemy-flag sighting r271 vs r232.

prerequisites.why: A spawn-held flag is defended for free by units respawning next to it. A relocated flag needs detection and convergence that do not depend on the spawn being next to it.
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the 15 that beat us: they pick up our flags 17 times a game to our 4. We kill their carriers 11 times a game vs 3, so carrier kills are above par. a2reloc vs those 15: our robots within dist2 20 of our flags at r300 fell from a mean of 10.0 to 5.5 (median 8.5 to 4). Their pickups went from 603 to 744 in total (median 15 to 20; more in 18 of 30 cells), and their captures from 67 to 73.

prerequisites.why: Respawns have to be routed to the relocated home to replace the free spawn-side defence.
prerequisites.evidence: Volume is at par (mean alive 44.9 vs 44.6). Routing is not: in Duck.trySpawn only defenders (index 0-2) respawn toward the relocated home, and other units go there only after an alert, which needs a robot within dist2 20 of the home to see an enemy. The defend300 drop from 10.0 to 5.5 above is the measured effect. Marked below par for this tactic, not in general.

prerequisites.why: Adoption needs the enemy spawn centroid at r2-3 to choose 'far from the enemy'. Neutralization (finding their relocated flags) is C1 directly.
prerequisites.evidence: Census first flag sighting r271 vs r232. Symmetry comes only from the broadcast hints at r1-3 (Sym.fromBroadcasts); if those are ambiguous, the code defaults to rotation. How often that happens is unknown (guess). Neutralization cost, measured: vs flag movers that beat us our first sighting is r275 vs r266 for non-movers. By the opponent's flagMoveDist, our median first pickup is r257 at 0 vs r265 at 30+, our first capture r398 vs r466, and mean captures 2.01 vs 1.58. Within the same opponent (small n, maps confounded), our first pickup vs Gymhgy is r265.5 (n=12) vs r337 (n=14), and vs chenyx r312 (n=5) vs r398 (n=21). Our win rate is 14% vs movers that beat us and 17% vs non-movers that beat us, so relocated enemy flags are not a primary cause of our losses.

prerequisites.why: A carrier moves at +20 cooldown and cannot act, so it cannot fill water and must path around it. A behind-water target needs a land path.
prerequisites.evidence: Sufficient for the plain version: 108 of 110 placements succeeded (DefaultHuge diagnostic: placed at r23, r44 and r76; the RELOC_STALL fallback exists). Not measured against opponents. Probably not sufficient for behind-water targets without path memory (guess).

prerequisites.why: The new home has to be published so that alerts, defence, ring traps and respawns all use it.
prerequisites.evidence: By code inspection: Comms slots 20-22 (OF_HOME) are written on the drop, and Comms.flagHome is used by sense(), defend(), trySpawn() and fieldTarget(). It works in a2reloc. Nothing compares it with opponents.

prerequisites.why: Setup digging turns land into water, so it may be how some movers make 'behind water' moats around a relocated flag. This is a guess: the co-occurrence is measured, the mechanism is not traced.
prerequisites.evidence: 4 of the 6 movers that beat us dig at least 20 tiles in setup (Gymhgy 60, chenyx 90, hsmalladi 60, uravt 21.5). None of the 9 movers we beat do. Our digs by r200: 0 (a3dig5 84/110 and a3dig10 82/110 vs control 84/110 were neutral).

prerequisites.why: A relocated flag held by 1 defender needs standing defences (traps) more than a spawn-side one.
prerequisites.evidence: Census traps built 187.5 vs 239, trap hit rate 0.86 vs 0.92. Removing the flag ring (ab2noring) read 20-19, i.e. worth about nothing. The fortress ring d3fort read 16-29 vs arch_rush10.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
Moving the flags is easy and our copy did it (108 of 110 games, median flagMoveDist 26). What decides whether it pays is several below-par capabilities plus one we do not have. In the paired a2reloc vs g_iter1-control cells (same 110 cells, SEED 424242, progress/survey.csv), relocation did the one thing it can do: it delayed losses. The control's 6 CAPTURE losses before r500 (r353-482) became 0; the fastest relocated loss was r529, and the opponent's median first capture moved from r348.5 to r420. It did not slow the first raid (opponent's median first pickup r269 vs r268.5) and did not reduce enemy captures (90 vs 87 in all cells).

The delay was not converted, for two reasons.
(1) Offence. Against the 15 bots that beat us, our pickups rose from a median of 3.5 to 6.5 (higher in 21 of 30 cells), but captures stayed at 0. In the 8 fast-loss twins we captured 0-2 flags in the 85-1600 extra rounds. C8 conversion (0.06 vs 0.13) and C11 territory (10 vs 24 in the enemy half at r250) are the binding gaps. A delay is only worth something inside a flag race we can win.
(2) Defence. Moving flags away from spawn removes the free defence of respawning units. Our robots near our flags at r300 fell from a mean of 10.0 to 5.5, and enemy pickups rose from 603 to 744 and captures from 67 to 73. C10 and C6 respawn routing did not adapt: only defenders respawn toward the new home.

Also, our copy was not hsmalladi's tactic. The placement had no terrain memory (straight-line grid, edge tiles x,y<2 excluded, nothing behind water). It moved flags only about 9 tiles each, and the broadcast hint still points raiders at them.

The test itself was also weak. 80 of the 110 field cells were against bots we beat almost always (78 vs 77 wins there), leaving 30 informative cells: 0 gained, 4 lost, sign test p about 0.125. TRAINING_LOG recorded only win counts, not the mechanism metrics above. The arch_rush10 check (20-21) used our own below-par flag finding as the raider.

Verdict: the test shows that plain relocation on g_iter1 is not a free win. It cannot judge terrain-aware relocation or relocation inside a stronger flag-race offence. Survey context: the movers that beat us also raid hard (they pick up our flags 26 times a game vs 15 for non-movers that beat us), and 4 of 6 also dig in setup. So T2 looks like part of a raid-race package (T1/T3/T4), not a standalone lever.
buildOrder: C8 capture conversion: turn the pickups we already make into captures (a2reloc raised our pickups 3.5 to 6.5 vs the top bots with 0 more captures; capture rate 0.06 vs 0.13)
C11 territory/tempo: more robots in the enemy half after the dam opens (10 vs 24 at r250), so that time bought at home turns into a flag race we win

C10 + C6 defence of a flag away from spawn: early warning and respawn routing to the relocated home for all units, not just the 3 defenders, so robots near our flags at r300 do not fall from 10.0 to 5.5

NEW terrain memory / path distance: store walls and water as they are sensed and call the unused Sym.observe; score placements by land-path distance from the enemy; allow edge and corner tiles; prefer spots behind water
C13 setup digging for moats around relocated flags (optional, guess: 4 of 6 movers that beat us dig at least 20 tiles in setup, none of the movers we beat do)
Retry T2 on the rating band (240 games), logging the opponent's first pickup and first capture per flag, robots near our flags at r300, and our captures in the extra rounds, not only win counts

decompositions.name: Flag relay (carrier hands the flag forward to an adjacent ally)

prerequisites.why: Basic carry and the drop/pickup mechanics. Rules (RULES.md, Flags and Actions tables): a carrier moves at +20 cooldown, so 0.5 tiles/round. A drop costs +10 action and +10 move, a pickup costs +10 action, and a dropped flag cannot be picked up again until the next round. The best a relay can do is one homeward move plus one homeward drop per 2 rounds, i.e. 1 tile/round, and only if a fresh, action-ready taker is next to the next tile every cycle. An unclaimed flag returns home after 4 ticks.
prerequisites.evidence: Census (700 g_iter1 games; research/census-g_iter1*.csv): carrier moves per carrier-round 0.48 for us vs 0.45 (median) for the bots that beat us. Captures per pickup vs those bots: 0.11 for us vs 0.11 for them (sums: 0.63/5.5 vs 2.30/21.8 per game). The drop/pickup code works mechanically: the a2relay arm logged 44,439 drops in 110 games. Caveat: carrierSpeed counts robot moves per holding round, so it cannot see a relay's flag-speed gain at all.

prerequisites.why: Opponents relay a few times per capture, probably when the carrier is hurt or threatened or an escort is ready. Our version relays every time any ally is within dist2 2 of a tile closer to home. Nothing checks HP, threat, or whether the taker can act.
prerequisites.evidence: src/bot/Duck.java relay() (around lines 224-244), called from carryFlag() every turn when C.RELAY is on. From progress/survey.csv, drops per capture: a2relay 219 (median 192 drops/game, up to 1818) vs kuma 6.4, Gymhgy 7.2, NotLLeon 3.0, hsmalladi 2.8. Within kuma, Gymhgy and NotLLeon, high-drop games capture no more than low-drop ones (2.57 vs 2.64, 2.93 vs 2.57, 2.69 vs 2.67). Strong non-relayers capture as much with 0 drops: andrewgopher (median 0, 24 of 28 games with 0), jmerle 2.96, Strequals 3.00, CyrilSharma 2.57, andli28 2.43 captures/game.

prerequisites.capability: NEW:route continuity across holders (shared or deterministic homeward path / distance field)
prerequisites.why: Each new holder has to keep moving the flag along the same path, and the drop tile has to be the next tile on that path, not just a tile that is closer in a straight line. Otherwise the flag bounces back and forth near walls and water. A carrier cannot fill water, because carrying blocks every action except moving.
prerequisites.evidence: src/bot/Nav.java is greedy plus bug-following, and its state (bugging, bugDir, bestDist, and handedness from id parity) belongs to each robot, so every hand-off throws it away. relay() drops on the tile with the smallest straight-line dist2 to the nearest spawn tile. In the a2relay block, drops per game by map: open maps HungerGames 8, Skyline 23, Ambush 66; walled or watery maps MazeRunner 626, Funnel 682, Digging 908, SteamboatMickey 1384, Rainbow 1784, Duck 1818. Captures, relay vs control: Funnel 9 vs 16, BigDucksBigPond 3 vs 6, Digging 1 vs 3. The ping-pong mechanism is my inference; it has not been traced in a replay.

prerequisites.why: Someone has to take the flag. Escorts must stand on the carrier's homeward side, next to the next route tile, while the carrier is under fire. Without escort formation the relay only fires when allies happen to be nearby.
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the 15 bots that beat us: carrier deaths per pickup 0.87 for us (4.8 deaths on 5.5 pickups per game) vs 0.66 for them (their denominator is inflated by relay pickups; corrected, my guess is about 0.55-0.65 for kuma/Gymhgy). Medians: their carriers are killed 11 times a game by us, ours 3 times by them, on 17 vs 4 pickups. Code: in fieldTarget() (Duck.java), escorting a visible friendly carrier is the last priority, and any duck with an enemy in view goes to Micro.fight instead.

prerequisites.why: The payoff base. A relay only acts during a carry, and against the bots that beat us we rarely carry.
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the 15 that beat us: robots in the enemy half at r250, 10 for us vs 24 for them (18 vs 13 in our wins); pickups (medians) 4 vs 17, sums 5.5 vs 21.8 per game; captured 0 vs 3. Conversion per pickup is equal (0.11 vs 0.11), so the whole flag gap is pickup volume, which a relay does not touch.

prerequisites.why: Finding enemy flags early raises the number of carries a relay could speed up.
prerequisites.evidence: First enemy-flag sighting r271 vs r232 (bots that beat us); r228.5 vs r231.5 against bots we beat.

prerequisites.why: The carrier cannot see an ally's cooldowns (RobotInfo does not include them). A taker who just attacked (+20) or healed (+30) cannot pick up. A shared-array handshake or a reserved escort role that keeps its action free would make hand-offs reliable.
prerequisites.evidence: Code inspection: Comms.java has slots for our-flag carry sightings (OF_CARRY) but nothing for our own carriers, escorts or hand-offs. relay() accepts any ally within dist2 2 of the drop tile, whatever that ally's state.

prerequisites.why: Single-robot navigation quality sets the pace of a normal carry and of the escorts moving ahead of it.
prerequisites.evidence: No navigation comparison against opponents in the census. Plateau audit of 40 g_iter1 replays: still 32.6%, ABA 9.4%. Single-carrier pace is at par (0.48 vs 0.45 moves per carrier-round).

prerequisites.why: A raid squad (T1/T12) supplies escorts near the carrier, which is where opponents' relays seem to happen (guess).
prerequisites.evidence: arch_rush10 (squad plus relay): 84/110 = control. fl10 (flank squad plus relay): 20-23 over 2 band seeds; fl6 7-11 on one seed. Both carry the same defective relay (arch_rush10: 458 drops/game median, 198 captures vs control 241 on the same cells).

prerequisites.why: The escorts have to survive the fight around the carrier.
prerequisites.evidence: Kills vs the bots that beat us: 245.5 vs 292 overall, 212 vs 220 in our losses (roughly even).

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
The test was inadequate twice over. It did not test the tactic opponents use, and its outcome measure could not see the harm the arm actually did.

(1) What was tested: an always-on relay, not the sparing hand-off the opponents use. I paired a2relay against its control on the same 110 cells (progress/survey.csv, run 20260930-182523-scrim-a2relay vs 20260930-183700-scrim-g_iter1).
- Drops: median 192 per game, mean 404, 219 per capture. Opponents drop 3-7 times per capture.
- Captures: 203 vs 241. The relay captured fewer in 37 cells and more in 8.
- Win types: CAPTURE wins (all 3 flags) fell from 67 to 43. MORE_FLAG_CAPTURES wins rose from 13 to 32.
- First capture came a median 28.5 rounds later (later in 51 cells, earlier in 31).
- Against the bots that beat us (30 cells): 13 captures vs 24, wins 3 vs 7.
So the arm was not neutral. It slowed flag delivery. Likely mechanism (inferred from the code and the per-map pattern, not traced): each hand-off throws away the per-robot bug-nav state, and relay() drops toward the tile closer in straight-line distance to the nearest spawn. Around walls and water the flag bounces back and forth. Drops run 8-70 per game on open maps and 600-1800 on mazy or watery maps (Duck 1818, Rainbow 1784).

(2) The judge hid the damage. A full-field win count resolves about +-5 games, and most cells are against bots we beat anyway at r2000 on flag count. On those cells we won 78 vs 77 despite 190 vs 217 captures. No diagnostic of the ry counter (relay drops) or drops per capture was logged before the block.

(3) Even a correct relay had little to work with. Against the bots that beat us we convert pickups as well as they do (0.11 captures per pickup). The gap is pickup volume (5.5 vs 21.8 per game) and presence in the enemy half (10 vs 24 robots at r250), which the relay does not touch. Five top bots capture 2.4-3.0 flags a game with 0 drops.

(4) Consequence: the same defective relay runs inside arch_rush10 (458 drops/game, 198 captures vs 241) and the T12 arms fl6/fl10. Their neutral results partly price this defect. The log line "arch_rush keeps the relay, which fed its captures" is not supported by these numbers.

One hint, but confounded: up2 (CAPTURING first, carriers at +12, about 0.83 tiles/round, faster than any relay without coordination) went 14-33. That suggests carrier speed is not the binding constraint, but up2 also delayed the ATTACK upgrade, so it is not a clean test.
buildOrder: Instrument first (not a capability, but it gates the retry): add flag-delivery metrics to --capabilities: drops per capture, flag tiles toward home per carried round, rounds from pickup to capture. Make any relay arm show 3-10 drops per capture in a diagnostic before it gets a block. Re-run arch_rush10 and fl10 with C.RELAY=false to unconfound the T1/T12 results.

C11 territory/tempo with C1 flag localisation: more bodies in the enemy half (10 vs 24 at r250) and earlier sightings (r271 vs r232), to raise pickups (5.5 vs 21.8 per game). This is the payoff base; without it a relay has nothing to accelerate.
C9 escort formation: escort a friendly carrier above fighting and exploring, positioned on its homeward side. Target carrier deaths per pickup at about 0.66 or below (now 0.87).

NEW route continuity: one homeward distance field (BFS from our spawn zones, computed once per robot and deterministic, or shared). Every holder and every drop follows it, and it avoids water the carrier cannot fill.

Hand-off policy with C7: relay only when the carrier is hurt or threatened, or when a confirmed action-ready escort is on the next route tile. Use a shared-array handshake or a reserved escort role. Then retest as a paired gate and on the rating band, judging on captures and first-capture round as well as wins.

decompositions.name: Setup digging for build XP (level-sum tiebreak, cheaper traps)

prerequisites.why: Each dig costs 20 crumbs, so 55-90 digs cost 1100-1800 crumbs in setup. The diggers that beat us pay that and still bank for the fight. Our arm could only dig while the bank was at least 1020 (DIG_RESERVE 1000, Duck.java:182), and our bank is almost never that high in setup.
prerequisites.evidence: Survey: our crumbs250 is 240; diggers that beat us bank 1092-6650 (6 of the 8 bank at least 1000). Our crumbs200 is 175 (control); theirs is 825-6222 for kuma, Strequals, andli28, CyrilSharma and hsmalladi. Census: gathered200 is at par (3200 vs 3000) but gathered400 is not (3900 vs 4950). Effect on the arm: median digs200 was 0 in both arms; 64/110 (a3dig5) and 62/110 (a3dig10) games had zero digs, and dose 10 averaged 26.8 digs against 24.0 for dose 5.

prerequisites.why: Opponents spend their setup actions on digs instead of setup traps. They aim for an exact XP target (about 5 digs = build level 1 per digging duck) and dig where it does not get in their way. We dug on top of our setup-trap habit, stopped part-way when the bank ran out, and used a checkerboard over our whole territory, including the dam front. setupDig runs before the GATHER_ROUND branch (Duck.java:160). Its docstring says dam-adjacent tiles are skipped, but no code does that.
prerequisites.evidence: Diggers dig in 28 of 28 games (zero fraction 0.0). They make 55-90 digs and reach level200 11-18 with level200 = digs200/5 (kuma 90/18, Strequals 90/18, chenyx 90/18, hsmalladi 60/12, Gymhgy 60/12, CyrilSharma 55/11), so it looks like exactly build L1 on 11-18 ducks (inference). They build 0-6 setup traps; we build 29-33. In the arm's delivered games, paired against the control cell: +79 digs gave only +5.5 level200 (ideal about +16) and traps200 fell by 17, so dig XP replaced trap XP instead of adding to it.

prerequisites.why: Water we dig in our own territory sits in our own paths. Nav.fillToward fills water as soon as the greedy step and both side steps fail, before it tries bug navigation (Nav.java:44, 64-72). Filling costs 30 crumbs, gives no XP, and FILL_RESERVE is 0. So our ducks paid to undo our own digs.
prerequisites.evidence: In the arm's delivered games (digs200 >= 20, 32 per arm), paired against the same control cells: fills200 rose by 30.1 (a3dig5) and 31.5 (a3dig10), about 900 crumbs; crumbs200 fell by 710 and 790. The control already fills 35-45 tiles by r200 (about 1000-1350 crumbs). Diggers fill 16-101 by r200, about what we fill, although they dig 55-90; where they dig is unmeasured (it needs replay boards).

prerequisites.why: The 'cheaper traps' payoff is 10% off traps at build level 1 and 15% off at level 2, plus 5-10% faster build cooldown (engine SkillType.java). It only pays a duck that builds many traps in fights. Five digs cost 100 crumbs and save about 10 per later stun, so they break even only after roughly 10 traps per duck (computed, not measured).
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the bots that beat us: trapsBuilt 187.5 vs 239, trapsHit 149.5 vs 221. That is about 4-5 traps per duck per game for us, below break-even. The diggers that beat us reach stun400 of 60-139 (CyrilSharma 139). The ablation ab4nocombat lost 16-26, so combat stun traps are load-bearing. In the arm's delivered games stun400 fell by 19 (a3dig5) and 22 (a3dig10), and kills fell by 78 and 97 against the control cell: digging took money from the one trap habit that matters.

prerequisites.why: The trap-discount half of T4 only pays inside T5 (bank through setup, trap in the fight). Among the opponents that beat us, the two tactics come together, and T5 is itself still neutral for us. Without T5 there is neither a setup bank to dig from nor combat-trap volume for the discount to multiply.
prerequisites.evidence: Of the 8 diggers that beat us, 6 bank at least 1000 at r250, 5 are stun-heavy, and none builds 15 or more setup traps. Our attempts at T5 were neutral: c5bank 82/110 and c6pair 82/110 vs control 84. c5bank shows a bank is reachable (crumbs200 median 1075). The dig arms were built on g_iter1 and never stacked on a bank arm.

prerequisites.why: The level-sum half pays only in r2000 games with equal flag counts. That headroom is small, and on the test cells it was zero.
prerequisites.evidence: Census, 590 games: 58 ended on LEVEL_SUM; we won 46 and lost 12 (2.0% of games). 9 of the 12 losses were to setup diggers (hsmalladi 3, kuma 2, Gymhgy 2, Strequals 1, andli28 1). In those games MORE_FLAG_CAPTURES losses were 119, ten times more. On the 110-game field cells used for the test, the control went 7-0 on LEVEL_SUM, a3dig5 3-0 and a3dig10 3-1. Our level200 is 4-6 vs 11-18 for the diggers. The a3dig5 diagnostic won 421-419 on level sum, the kind of margin digging can swing. Level sum at r2000 is not in the census CSVs.

prerequisites.why: Reaching level 4 in one skill caps the other skills at level 3. At dose 10, a trap-heavy duck reaches build L4 (20 XP) and can no longer reach heal mastery, which iteration 10 found valuable. The jail penalty also strips XP from a duck's highest skill, so the level sum depends on deaths.
prerequisites.evidence: Engine rule (RULES.md, InternalRobot.incrementSkill). In g_iter1's long games about 40 of 50 ducks reach heal mastery first (iteration 10, --levels). The dig arms have no --levels data, so this interaction is a guess. Survival is at par (deaths 220 vs kills 212 in our losses; meanAlive 44.9 vs 44.8).

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
Both. The test was inadequate, and where the tactic did fire, its prerequisites were missing.

(1) The test was inadequate: the treatment was mostly not delivered.
- The dig gate (bank at least 1020, DIG_RESERVE 1000) almost never opens for us, because we spend crumbs in setup (crumbs200 median 175).
- Median digs200 was 0 in both arms; 64/110 and 62/110 games had no digs.
- Digging happened only on crumb-rich maps (Skyline 235/443, Joker 234/227, StarryNight, CH3353C4K3F4CT0RY, Snake, Battlecode24): 32 games per arm.
- Dose 10 averaged 26.8 digs against 24.0 for dose 5. 'No dose response' is therefore a non-result, because the two doses were never different.
- In the delivered games the paired flips were 2-1 and 1-2, far below the instrument's resolution.
- The judge was the old 110-game full-field block (before the switch to the rating band). On those cells the control lost no LEVEL_SUM games (7-0), so the tiebreak channel had nothing to win.
- Even a perfect version has a low ceiling on the tiebreak channel. LEVEL_SUM losses are 12 of 590 census games, about 5 games in a 240-game band block, against roughly 17-23 flips each way between any two builds.

(2) Missing prerequisites. In the games where it did dig, the arm hurt the load-bearing channel. Paired against the control on the same cells:
- crumbs200 fell by 710 to 790;
- fills200 rose by about 30: Nav filled our own dug water at 30 crumbs each, for no XP;
- traps200 fell by 17;
- stun400 fell by 19 to 22, and kills fell by 78 to 97;
- level200 rose only 5.5 for 79 extra digs, because dig XP replaced setup-trap XP and partial dig counts gave no level.

What the opponents do is different (inference from the survey). They dig unconditionally (100% of games), about 5 per digging duck (level200 = digs200/5), instead of setup traps (0-6), while banking 1000-6650 crumbs. They then spend the bank on combat stuns (60-139 by r400), where the 10-15% trap discount pays.

We copied the visible action, but not the setup budget (C3/C13), the nav that tolerates the water (C2), or the bank-then-spend channel (T5/C5) that the dig pays into. A guess, not measured: dam-front digging from r150 (setupDig runs during the gather phase, and the promised dam skip is not implemented) may also have slowed our own push.
buildOrder: C2: own-water-aware nav. Try bug navigation before filling, never refill tiles we dug, and track fills200 (control 35-45 by r200, about 1000-1350 crumbs). This also frees crumbs for C3.
C3: setup bank discipline. Raise crumbs250 from about 240 toward 1000 or more without losing the fight; c5bank already reached a crumbs200 median of 1075.
C5 / T5: combat-trap spending that turns the bank into fight traps. Targets: trapsBuilt 187 vs 239, stun400 toward the 60-139 the diggers reach. The trap discount pays only here.

C13: dig placement and XP targeting. Dig exactly 5 per duck (build L1, never past L3 so heal mastery stays possible), only on ducks expected to trap, in place of setup traps rather than in addition, with no 1000 reserve gate, and on tiles off our own lanes (not the dam front).

Instrumentation before retrying: add digs200, level200 and level sum at r2000 to the capability census. Run a delivery check first: digs in at least 90% of games, level200 rising by about digs/5, fills200 not rising.
Then retry T4 stacked on the best T5 arm on the rating band with 4 or more seeds, with a pre-registered estimate of LEVEL_SUM flips (ceiling about 5 per 240 games).

decompositions.name: Bank through setup, trap in the fight

prerequisites.why: The bank at r200 comes from not spending in setup, not from gathering more. Opponents gather less than we do by r200 (3000 vs our 3200) yet hold 2850 to our 175, because they build no setup traps. Doing T5 means spending nothing on setup traps.
prerequisites.evidence: survey.csv, g_iter1 vs the 16 that beat us (64 games): traps200 32.5 vs 1.5, crumbs200 175 vs 2851; fills200 34 vs 33 (at par). The c5bank arm still built 24.5 setup traps (c6pair 23.5) vs the opponents' 2.0 and 1.5, because the flag ring stayed on. Ablations price setup traps near 0 (ab1nodam 20-16, ab2noring 20-19), so dropping them costs nothing. Setup digs (build XP, -10% trap cost at build level 1 per engine SkillType) are 0 for us vs 55-90 for kuma, Strequals, andli28 and CyrilSharma; level200 is 4-6 vs 11-18.

prerequisites.why: Crumbs are one team pool that every duck reads with getCrumbs(). To bank, every spender has to obey one paced budget. To trap in the fight, crumbs have to keep coming in after r200. We have neither: five separate per-spender floors (FILL_RESERVE 0, DEF_TRAP_RESERVE 100, DAM_TRAP_RESERVE 600, TRAP_RESERVE 200, FLOAT_CRUMBS 1500), and the lowest active floor sets the bank.
prerequisites.evidence: Gathering in setup is at par (gathered200 3200 vs 3000); banking, pacing and post-setup income are not. All three bank arms sit at crumbs200 1052-1080, which is the DEF_TRAP_RESERVE 1000 cap: the ring turns every crumb above ~1100 into a trap. The opponents hold 2512-2655. At r250 c5bank holds 277, which is the TRAP_RESERVE 200 floor plus one stun; c6pair holds 52 (floor 0). The opponents hold 1485-1855. So the bank was spent between r200 and r250, not paced. Crumbs gathered r200-r400 (per-game median, census, beater losses): 300 vs 1200; in our wins over beaters 200 vs 250. gathered400 3900 vs 4950.

prerequisites.why: This is the visible half of the tactic: 65-69 traps built during the fight by r400. Combat stun traps are load-bearing for us (ablation), but how many we build is limited by crumbs, not by the trigger rule.
prerequisites.evidence: Fight-phase traps (expl400+water400+stun400 minus traps200, per-game median vs beaters): g_iter1 24 vs 69, c5bank 38 vs 65, c6pair 39 vs 68. c6pair loosened the trigger (1 enemy, 0 reserve) and built the same number of traps as c5bank (3 enemies, 200 reserve), so supply binds, not the trigger. Ablation ab4nocombat 16-26; ct1 20-22, ct2 16-18, ct3 15-23. Placement quality is near par: trapHitRate 0.86 vs 0.92 (census).

prerequisites.why: Income during the fight is map crumbs in the centre and the enemy half, plus 30 crumbs per kill made while standing in enemy territory (engine InternalRobot.attack, KILL_CRUMB_REWARD). Being in the enemy half funds their fight traps and decides where traps get stepped on. Even a perfect setup bank leaves us about 15-20 fight traps short without this income.
prerequisites.evidence: inEnemy250 10 vs 24 and inEnemy300 10 vs 22 (census, beaters). The r200-r400 gathering gap shows up only in losses (300 vs 1200), not in wins (200 vs 250). Budget arithmetic, r200-r400: c5bank about 1065 bank + 2000 passive + 300 gathered ≈ 3400, about 38 stuns as observed. Opponents about 2850 + 2000 + 1200 + kill bounty ≈ 6000+, about 65-69 stuns as observed. The bounty size is a guess; the replay reader does not count it.

prerequisites.why: A team spend plan (rounds-to-phase budget, crumbs earmarked for the fight) is easiest with shared state. It is not strictly required: getCrumbs() is team-wide, so a deterministic round-paced floor that every spender obeys works without comms.
prerequisites.evidence: Comms.java schema has only IDX, EF_*, OF_ALERT, OF_LOC, SYM, OF_CARRY, OF_HOME; no economy or budget slot. Every spender in Duck.java and Nav.java checks rc.getCrumbs() against its own constant.

prerequisites.why: Traps pay only if the fight is held where enemies step forward. The combat trap is built before Micro.fight at +5 action cooldown, so it rarely costs an attack.
prerequisites.evidence: Kills 212 vs 220 in our losses (census); in c6pair vs beaters kills 161.5 vs 156, and our traps triggered by them vs theirs triggered by us 167 vs 169: trap and kill parity reached.

prerequisites.why: How T5 turns into wins: the opponents' trap advantage pays off through flag pickups and captures. Our arm reached trap parity and nothing changed, because the decisive deficit is flags.
prerequisites.evidence: pickups 4 vs 17 and captureRate 0.06 vs 0.13 (census). c6pair vs beaters: 5/32 wins vs g_iter1's 12/64, 24 of 27 losses by CAPTURE, pickups 3 vs 15 even with trap and kill parity.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
Summary: the test was inadequate in two ways. The arm did not reproduce the tactic, and the block could not have detected an effect of the size involved. Where the arm did partly reproduce it, trap parity without territory moved nothing.

(1) The arm did not reproduce T5. Per survey.csv vs the 16 that beat us (32 games per arm):
- Setup traps stayed at 24.5 (c5bank) and 23.5 (c6pair) vs the opponents' 2 and 1.5.
- The r200 bank reached only ~1065 vs their ~2500-2650. DEF_TRAP_RESERVE=1000 is a reserve on a shared pool, so it works as a cap: defenders turn every crumb above ~1100 into flag-ring traps. All three bank arms sit at 1052-1080.
- The bank was gone by r250: c5bank 277 (the TRAP_RESERVE 200 floor plus one stun), c6pair 52, vs 1485-1855 for the opponents. TACTICS.md says "the combat-trap rule does not spend the bank", but the data says the opposite: it spent the bank at once rather than pacing it.
- FLOAT_CRUMBS 1500 stayed on. FILL_RESERVE 500 never bound: fills200 33.5 vs 34 for g_iter1, because the bank sat at ~1000. The water-heavy-map fill drain is not the median story.

(2) The net change was small and limited by crumbs. About 8 setup traps moved into about 14 more fight traps: r200-r400 traps 24 to 38, vs the opponents' 65-69. c6pair's looser trigger (1 enemy, 0 reserve) built 39, the same as c5bank. So the fight-phase trap count is limited by crumbs, not by the trigger rule. ct1 and ct2 were neutral for the same reason. Budget arithmetic, r200-r400:
- Ours: ~1065 bank + 2000 passive + ~300 gathered ≈ 38 stuns.
- Theirs: ~2850 + 2000 + ~1200 gathered + 30-crumb kill bounties made in our territory ≈ 65+ stuns.
Even a perfect setup bank (~2850) leaves us ~15-20 fight traps short. The missing income is territory (C11: inEnemy250 10 vs 24; the r200-400 gathering gap appears only in losses, 300 vs 1200). Holding banks of 10775 (NotLLeon) and 17393 (CyrilSharma) at r250 are centre windfalls (T10), which is income and not withholding (ADVICE §11: large banks are usually a by-product of a snowball).

(3) Where the arm reached the tactic's measured outcome, wins did not move. In c6pair vs beaters, our traps triggered by them vs theirs triggered by us were 167 vs 169 and kills 161.5 vs 156, yet wins were 5/32 vs g_iter1's 12/64, 24 of 27 losses were by CAPTURE, and pickups were 3 vs 15. Out-trapping alone does not address the decisive deficit (C11/C8: flags and territory).

(4) Power: field blocks of 110 games, of which ~78 are near-certain wins (0.95-0.99). Only ~32 games per arm are against the bots that show T5. The log notes any two builds flip ~10 games each way. A 4-gained/6-lost reading cannot separate a few-game effect from noise, and the 240-game band blocks were never run for c5bank or c6pair.

Verdict: the "bank through setup" half is elementary: do not spend in setup, which ablations say costs ~nothing, plus one paced floor. It was never tested cleanly. The "trap in the fight" half at the opponents' volume needs post-setup income from territory and pays off only through flag play. Both are below par, which makes the whole tactic composite. Guess, not measured: the bank-only half correctly done would gain ~10-14 fight traps and land at +0-3 games per 240, below what the band can resolve.
buildOrder: C3 pacing: replace the five per-spender floors (FILL/DEF_TRAP/DAM_TRAP/TRAP reserves, FLOAT_CRUMBS) with one round-paced team floor that every spender obeys; float traps off. Gate it on the signature, not on win rate, over a few diagnostic games: traps200 <= 6, crumbs200 >= 2500, crumbs250 >= 1000, fight traps r200-400 >= 50

C13: zero setup traps (ab1nodam/ab2noring price them ~0); optionally ~5 setup digs per duck for build level 1 (-10% trap cost). T4 alone was neutral, so treat it as a cost reduction for T5, not as a lever

C11 territory/tempo: raise robots in the enemy half at r250 from 10 toward ~20. This is the post-setup income T5's trap volume needs (map crumbs plus the 30-crumb kill bounty in enemy territory) and the census's main deficit
C5: once supply is no longer the limit, aim combat traps for an advancing line (trap ahead of the push) and track hit rate 0.86 -> 0.92
C8/C10 conversion check, then retry T5 on 240-game band blocks (2 seeds), scored on pickups and captures as well as wins

decompositions.name: Attack-heavy fighting (top bots attack more and heal less than we do by r400)

prerequisites.why: Attack volume is duck-turns with an enemy within dist2 4 and the action ready. The side that is forward chooses where and when contact happens. The defending side fights near its own spawn with damaged and respawning ducks, so it heals more. Our attack count flips with the outcome, as territory does.
prerequisites.evidence: Census, vs the 15 that beat us: inEnemy250 10 vs 24 (in our wins it flips to 18 vs 13). Survey, vs the top 16 (363-384 games, g_iter1-family builds): in our wins we attack 1085 vs their 714; in our losses 875 vs 942. In the 110-game block where survey and census join: rho(attack diff, inEnemy250 diff) = 0.59 and rho(attack diff, won) = 0.61. In its 32 top-16 games the same figures are 0.26 and 0.32.

prerequisites.why: A stun trap sets enemy move and action cooldowns to 40 (RULES.md), so stunned ducks cannot attack for 3-4 turns and are free targets. The side ahead on stuns gets more attacks and suffers fewer. The 10 top bots that are stun-heavy are mostly the same bots that out-attack us.
prerequisites.evidence: Survey vs the top 16: stun400 55 vs 68. Per game, rho(their-minus-our atk400, their-minus-our stun400) = 0.60 (n = 363). Census: their traps hit us 221 times, ours hit them 149.5; hit rate 0.92 vs 0.86. Ablation ab4nocombat 16-26: combat stuns are load-bearing. Quantity knobs ct1/ct2/ct3 were flat or worse, so the gap is in effectiveness, not in count.

prerequisites.why: Micro turns contact and stun windows into attacks. Micro.fight kites to dist2 11-20. It engages only when the duck is action-ready and either locally strong or facing at most ENGAGE_MAX_THREAT threats. Targets are chosen locally: carriers first, then lowest HP.
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the top 15: kills 245.5 vs deaths 292 overall, but 212 vs 220 in our losses (even). atk400 vs the top 16: 884 vs 922 in the survey and 807 vs 975 in the block study. Micro v2 lost 1-25: the current lexicographic micro is a local optimum, not a broken one.

prerequisites.why: A heal costs 30 cooldown and blocks 2 turns, while an attack costs 20 and blocks 1. The engage branch needs actReady. A duck that heals while an enemy is one or two steps from reach therefore cannot strike when the enemy steps in. This is the only part of T6 that is a knob in its own right.
prerequisites.evidence: Code: tryHeal runs on any ally below HEAL_HP_BELOW = 1000 whenever the duck is action-ready with nothing in reach (Micro.fight, and every non-fight branch of Duck.turn), with no check for enemy proximity. We heal 1.34 times per enemy attack; they heal 1.19 times per ours. We take more total actions than they do (2135 vs 1908) yet make fewer attacks. GUESS: part of the attack gap is heals spent just before contact. Nothing measures this.

prerequisites.why: The crumb bank funds the combat stuns of C5. Ten of the 16 top bots are stun-heavy and 11 bank crumbs.
prerequisites.evidence: Census: gathered400 3900 vs 4950. Survey: crumbs250 ~240 vs 1000-6650 for the bankers. rho(attack gap, crumbs250 gap) = 0.22 (weak). Banking alone (c5bank, c6pair) was neutral, 82/110 vs 84.

prerequisites.why: The army has to know where the enemy flags and the front are before it can hold the enemy half (C11).
prerequisites.evidence: Census: firstFlagSight r271 vs r232 against the bots that beat us; r235.5 vs 231 in our wins.

prerequisites.why: Focus fire through a shared target slot raises kills per attack, and broadcasting the battlefront sends reinforcements to the live fight (ADVICE section 13).
prerequisites.evidence: Comms.java uses about 23 slots, for flag IDs and locations, alerts, carriers and symmetry. There is no combat target or battlefront slot, and bestTarget looks only at what one duck can see.

prerequisites.why: Attack volume needs bodies. Equal headcount rules out a headcount explanation (ADVICE: check unit-count parity before blaming trade efficiency).
prerequisites.evidence: Census: meanAlive 44.9 vs 44.6 against the bots that beat us.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
T6 is not a behaviour the top bots share. It is an aggregate statistic that comes out of how fights go, and the adoption test was also too weak to show an effect.

(1) The statistic is not a tactic. Only 4 of the 16 top bots attack more than they heal. TACTICS.md's own T8 row says 10 of 16 heal more than they attack, the opposite profile for the same population. 10 of 16 out-attack us and 13 of 16 heal less than we do. Our heal count is a response to damage taken: rho(our heal400, their atk400) = 0.72 vs the top 16 and 0.92 over all games, about 1.34 heals per enemy attack. So "we heal more" mostly means "they hit us more". Absolute attack volume flips with the outcome (in our wins vs the top 16 we attack 1085 vs their 714; in losses 875 vs 942). It tracks territory (rho 0.59 overall) and stun traps (rho 0.60). Those are below-par capabilities C11 and C5, with C3 and C1 beneath them. None of the knobs touched them.

(2) The knobs barely produced the profile they were meant to produce, and nobody checked. Per-cell paired deltas vs the top 16 against the control block: e1aggr (ADVANCE_MARGIN 3 to 1) raised our atk400 by +49 (about 5%), but heal400 also rose (+41) and their attacks rose (+11). e2aggr raised atk400 by +26 with heals +2. The gap to close was about 170 attacks in the block study. The knobs act only in narrow branches of Micro.fight: ADVANCE_MARGIN only when no enemy is reachable from the candidate tile, ENGAGE_MAX_THREAT only when locally outnumbered. Neither touches the heal-whenever-ready rule, stun traps or territory.

(3) The test lacked power. These were field blocks of 110 games, and only 32 were against the 16 bots that show T6 (2 per opponent). We win the other 78 at about 97%. The log says this instrument resolves about 5 games, and 83 and 81 vs 84 sit inside that. The same g_iter1 build read 81 and 84 on two field blocks with different cells. The arms were never run on the 240-game rating band.

(4) The "no dose response" headline hides opposite signs. Paired on identical cells, e1 went 1 gained / 5 lost vs the top 16 and 3 / 0 vs the rest; e2 went 1 / 6 and 2 / 0. This is a post-hoc subgroup and the two arms are correlated (e2 includes e1), so treat it as a lean, not a result. More aggression without stun, bank and territory support seems to lose fights to exactly the bots that show T6, which fits the culminating-point advice.

The conclusion that this is a symptom and not a knob is right, but this test could not have reached any other verdict. A retry needs the prerequisites first, plus a manipulation check: our atk400 up and heal400 down vs the top 16.
buildOrder: Instrument first (not a bot capability): in the replay reader, add per-side r400 counts of duck-turns with an enemy within dist2 4 and action ready, stunned duck-turns, and heals made with an enemy within dist2 10. That splits the attack gap into contact time, stun and heal cooldown, and lets a retry check that its arm actually moved those counts.

C3 then C5: bank crumbs to fund combat stuns, then improve stun effectiveness and placement, not count. Today stun400 is 55 vs 68 and trap hits 149.5 vs 221; the per-game attack gap tracks the stun gap (rho 0.60). Measure quality: count-only knobs ct1 and ct2 read flat, ct3 worse.
C1 then C11: find the enemy flags earlier (first sighting r271 vs r232) and hold the enemy half at r250 (10 vs 24). This is the metric that flips in our wins, and our attack volume flips with it.

C4 action discipline (NEW), then C7 focus fire: no heal when an enemy can reach the duck within 2 turns unless the ally is critical. This is a cheap, elementary arm and can run early as a standalone diagnostic. Then add a shared focus-target slot and a battlefront broadcast in Comms.

Only then retry the T6 aggression dose (ADVANCE_MARGIN, ENGAGE_MAX_THREAT) on the 240-game rating band over 2 seeds, with a pre-registered manipulation check vs the top 16: our atk400 up, our heal400 down, their atk400 not up, inEnemy250 up.

decompositions.name: Centre crumb windfall, banked (sweep the dam-hidden crumbs r200-r225, bank them, out-trap over the fight)

prerequisites.why: The windfall goes to whichever side holds the centre in the first ~25 rounds after the dam drops, so territory is the gate. On HungerGames both sides first cross at r203, but the top bots have more bodies forward and take 85-95% of the crumbs.
prerequisites.evidence: inEnemy250 is 10 vs 24 against the bots that beat us (census n=444). On HungerGames inEnemy250 is 0-19 vs 17-42 and firstEnemySide 203 vs 203-208 (n=7). In the 238 census games with at least 4000 crumbs gathered r200-400, corr(our windfall share, inEnemy250 difference) = 0.52. Holding territory fixed, a high windfall share raises our win rate only when we are ahead on territory (0.27 -> 0.70, n=37/60); when behind or even it does not (0.23 vs 0.29, 0.32 vs 0.29). Observational data.

prerequisites.why: Gathering half: the crumbs have to be collected after the dam opens, while in contact with the enemy. Setup gathering is a separate matter and is at par.
prerequisites.evidence: gathered200 3200 vs 3000 (par). gathered400 3900 vs 4950. Gathered r200-400: median 300 vs 900 against the bots that beat us. 34% of band games (216/630) have a windfall; in those our share is 0.26 and the median deficit is 3200 crumbs. HungerGames gathered400: us 1200-4700, them 17500-21000 (NotLLeon 2600 vs 19600; uravt 2100 vs 20100).

prerequisites.why: The windfall race happens with enemies in view. Our crumb detour only fires when no enemy is in view, and the fight code never values crumb tiles.
prerequisites.evidence: In src/bot/Duck.java the enemies.length>0 branch (lines 29-35) returns before the POST_SETUP_CRUMBS detour (lines 39-42). src/bot/Micro.java has no crumb term (grep finds none). The detour counter 'cd' exists in G.java but was never reported for t10crumbs.

prerequisites.why: Banking and pacing half: a windfall-sized bank has to survive r225-r350 and be spent over the fight, not drained to the floor at once.
prerequisites.evidence: Bank at r250 is 250 vs 1910 against the bots that beat us (survey, g_iter1, n=60). Every banking arm reached ~1060 at r200 and lost it by r250: c4bank 265, c5bank 278 (FILL_RESERVE 500, FLOAT 1500, TRAP_RESERVE 200), c6pair 50-62 (TRAP_RESERVE 0). There is no team-wide rate limit: placeCombatTrap (Duck.java:460-462) fires for every duck with 3+ enemies in view and a bank of at least 300, and spendFloat fires above 1500. The only builds that ever held a bank on HungerGames are arch_rush (3185 and 4535 at r250), whose rush branch skips both spenders. NotLLeon and uravt bank 8.8k-17.6k there against almost every one of our builds.

prerequisites.why: The payoff: the bank is converted into stun traps that the enemy actually walks into, over the whole fight (NotLLeon 148 stun traps by r350).
prerequisites.evidence: Against the bots that beat us: trapsBuilt 187.5 vs 239, trapsHit 149.5 vs 221, hit rate 0.86 vs 0.92. On HungerGames: 44-83 traps built vs 158-332. Combat traps carry weight (ab4nocombat 16-26), but more of them does not help (ct1 20-22, ct2 16-18) and nearest-enemy aim is worse (ct3 15-23). So more crumbs only pay if trap quality improves too.

prerequisites.why: Sweeping the centre while in contact means surviving there; the trap advantage then has to turn into kills.
prerequisites.evidence: Kills 212 vs 220 in our losses and 245.5 vs 292 against the bots that beat us. meanAlive 44.9 vs 44.6 (C6 also at par).

prerequisites.why: A setup bank (the T5 sub-tactic) means traps can go down immediately at contact. NotLLeon reaches r200 with 2590 crumbs and 0 setup traps.
prerequisites.evidence: crumbs200 175 vs 2909 and traps200 34 vs 0.5 against the bots that beat us. Alone it is neutral: c5bank 82/110 vs control 84, ab1nodam 20-16, ab2noring 20-19.

prerequisites.why: Reaching and sweeping crumb tiles efficiently in the centre.
prerequisites.evidence: firstEnemySide 202 vs 202 (par for the first arrival). Our still% is 32.6 and ABA 9.4%, with no opponent comparison available.

prerequisites.why: A team-wide spend budget per round (for pacing) needs a shared counter, because crumbs are a shared pool and 47 ducks act independently.
prerequisites.evidence: Comms.java uses slots 0-22 of 64. Capacity is there, but there is no bank or budget field.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
Short answer: the test was inadequate, and the tactic also depends on prerequisites we are below par on. Neither arm ever produced the tactic's defining state, a windfall-sized bank around r225-r250.

(1) t10crumbs (src/t10crumbs/C.java: only POST_SETUP_CRUMBS=true) tested gathering only, and in the wrong place. The detour sits after the `enemies.length>0 ... return` branch in Duck.turn, so it fires only when no enemy is in view. The windfall race happens in contact, and Micro.fight never values crumb tiles. The arm also kept FLOAT_CRUMBS=1500, so any extra crumbs went straight into idle stun traps, which ab3nofloat shows are worth about 0. Its counter (cd) and its bank were never measured. The diagnostic behind the log's correction ("we collect the centre by walking over it") was against g_iter1, a mirror. Against the real users on HungerGames we gather 2100-2600 vs 19600-20100.

(2) ab3nofloat (only FLOAT_CRUMBS=1e6) does not test banking. The combat-trap rule (3+ enemies, bank >= 300) still drains every crumb. The c4/c5/c6 banking arms show this: about 1060 at r200, then 278/265/50 at r250. No survey or bank data exist for ab3nofloat, but by the same code it cannot have held a bank in fights.

(3) The payoff path is through C5, where quantity is not the lever (ct1 20-22, ct2 16-18). A bank would buy more of the traps that dose tests found neutral, unless trap quality and timing improve too.

(4) It is map-conditional and underpowered. Only 34% of band games have a windfall (at least 4000 crumbs gathered r200-400 by both sides). With about 43 discordant pairs a sign test needs 28-15 (net +13 of 240) for p<0.10, so even a large per-map effect would be diluted about 3x.

(5) It is composite. Our windfall share correlates 0.52 with the territory difference, and it helps only when we are already ahead on territory (win rate 0.27 -> 0.70; behind or even, no gain). That fits the cross-year advice that opponents' big banks are usually a by-product of a snowball, not a withholding policy. With C11 at 10 vs 24 robots in the enemy half at r250, a correct copy would still mostly lose the crumb race (a guess, based on correlation).
buildOrder: Instrument first (no capability change): for any T10 arm, report our share of crumbs gathered r200-250 and r200-400, the bank at r225/r250, crumbs spent per round and the cd counter, and score arms on the windfall-map subset (about 34% of band games) as well as the whole band
C11 territory/tempo: raise robots in the enemy half at r250 from 10 toward the opponents' 24. This is the gate: windfall share only pays when we are ahead on territory
In-contact crumb sweep (C3 gathering): give crumb tiles a value in Micro.fight and Nav when a tile is not threatened, so ducks sweep the dam line while fighting, not only when no enemy is in view

C3 pacing: a team-wide spend-rate limit (shared-array budget per round, or a bank floor that decays from r200), plus FLOAT_CRUMBS off. Check that the bank at r250 exceeds 1000 on windfall maps before judging any win rate
C5 trap quality: placement and timing that raise the hit rate from 0.86 toward 0.92 and land traps where enemies will step (volume alone is neutral)
Then retry T10 as one composite (territory + in-contact sweep + paced combat-trap spending), judged on windfall maps; C13 setup banking (the T5 piece) is an optional add-on

decompositions.name: Attack specialisation (attack mastery, levels 4-6)

prerequisites.capability: NEW:XP / skill-level steering (read own XP, hold back the action that would give a second skill level 4)
prerequisites.why: The engine caps the other skills at level 3 once any skill reaches level 4 (InternalRobot.incrementSkill). Heal level 4 needs 100 heals, so a duck can heal 99 times without losing any attack XP. Once its attack is level 4, its heal XP stops growing and it can heal freely again. The tactic is therefore a gate on one particular heal, which needs rc.getExperience / rc.getLevel. It is not a no-heal role.
prerequisites.evidence: src/bot never calls getExperience or getLevel. The only specialisation code is Micro.java:34 isAttacker() = idx%10 < C.ATTACKER_TENTHS (0 in src/bot), and tryHeal simply refuses for those ducks, forever. --levels (TRAINING_LOG iteration 10): about 40 of 50 g_iter1 ducks reach heal mastery first and about 1 reaches attack mastery; jonters.bling3 has 20. The sp5 diagnostic produced 22 masters vs 0 in self-play, but only 4-13 of 25 in two kuma losses. The census CSVs have no level metric.

prerequisites.why: Mastery multiplies damage per hit and attack rate, so it only pays if ducks land hits. Each duck needs 75/110/150 hits for attack level 4/5/6. Healing (also part of C4) is what the tested arm gave up.
prerequisites.evidence: Kills 245.5 vs deaths 292 vs the 15 bots that beat us; 212 vs 220 across all losses. Survey g_iter1 vs the top 15 (n=60): atk400 890 vs 958.5, heal400 1260 vs 872.5, which is 0.089 hits and 0.126 heals per duck per round over r200-400. At that rate, with no deaths, attack level 4 comes at about r1040, level 5 at about r1435, level 6 at about r1885 (extrapolation), while heal level 4 comes at about r993. MICRO_V2 was rejected 1-25, so the existing micro is strong.

prerequisites.why: Each death costs XP from the duck's highest skill: -5 at attack level 3-4, -10 at level 5, -12 at level 6 (SkillType.getPenalty). It also costs 25 rounds in jail with no hits. This delays mastery but does not reset it, contrary to the wording in TACTICS.md.
prerequisites.evidence: meanAlive 44.9 vs 44.6. Deaths per duck per game: 5.84 against the top 15, 5.16 in losses to them. At -5 XP per death that is about 26-29 XP lost, roughly +300 rounds to attack level 4 at 0.089 hits per round (estimate).

prerequisites.why: The payoff only starts at attack level 4, around r1040 without deaths and about r1350 with them. Games we lose on flags before then give the tactic all of its cost and none of its benefit. The time the tactic has to pay off is set by how long we keep our flags.
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the bots that beat us: enemy pickups 17 vs our 4; they capture 3 (median) in our losses; we kill their carriers 11 times a game and they kill ours 3. Of 374 g_iter1 losses to the top 15, 361 ended on flags (CAPTURE 249, MORE_FLAG_CAPTURES 112). Median loss ended r1083; 46% ended before r1000 and 57% before r1400.

prerequisites.why: This capability has to be protected, not raised. Level sum is our main way of beating top bots in long games. A duck that never heals gives up heal levels; the XP-gated version gives up none: heal 3 + attack 6 = 9, the same as heal 6 + attack 3.
prerequisites.evidence: 32 of our 70 wins against the top 15 came on LEVEL_SUM, against 12 of 374 losses. Level-sum margins at r2000 in TRAINING_LOG are small: 421-419 and 405-391. Guess: a never-heal duck loses about 3-4 levels compared with a healer (heal 4-6 + attack 3), so 45-100 team levels at sp3-sp5. End-of-game level sums are not in the census CSVs, so this is unmeasured.

prerequisites.why: More contact means more hits, which means faster attack XP. Kills only pay +30 crumbs when the attacker stands on enemy territory. Pushing forward also moves the fight away from our own flags.
prerequisites.evidence: Robots in the enemy half at r250: 10 vs 24 against the bots that beat us; this flips to 18 vs 13 in our wins.

prerequisites.capability: NEW:kill-breakpoint targeting (choose targets using own damage)
prerequisites.why: Mastery pays in steps of hits needed per kill. After the r600 ATTACK upgrade, level 3 (231 damage) needs 5 hits per 1000 HP, level 4 (273) needs 4, level 6 (336) needs 3. Before r600, level 3 (165) needs 7 and level 4 (195) needs 6. A targeting rule that ignores own damage wastes some of those steps.
prerequisites.evidence: Micro.bestTarget (Micro.java:19) ranks flag carriers first, then lowest HP, and ignores own damage. The one-hit-kill priority exists only in bestTargetV2, behind MICRO_V2=false. The census has no overkill or wasted-hit metric.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
The test was inadequate. It measured "never heal", which is not attack specialisation, and the tactic's payoff window lies mostly outside our typical loss.

(1) Wrong mechanism. For ducks with idx%10 < ATTACKER_TENTHS, Micro.tryHeal refuses every heal for the whole game. The engine cap (InternalRobot.incrementSkill) only fires when another skill reaches level 4, which for healing is the 100th heal. A specialist could have healed 99 times (heal level 3) at no cost to attack XP, and could heal freely again once attack reached level 4, because its heal XP is then frozen. Instead the arm gave up 30-70% of team healing from r200 onward. g_iter1 heals 0.126 times per duck per round over r200-400, 1260 heals by r400 against the top 15. The benefit only starts at attack level 4.

(2) Timing. At 0.089 hits per duck per round, attack level 4 comes at about r1040 (estimate), or about r1350 once the death penalty is counted (5.2-5.8 deaths per duck at -5 XP each). Our median loss to the top 15 ends at r1083; 46% end before r1000, and 97% end on flags. In about half our losses no specialist could have reached mastery.

(3) Hidden cost to level sum (guess, unmeasured). 32 of our 70 wins against the top 15 come on LEVEL_SUM, with r2000 margins as small as 2-14. A never-heal duck forgoes heal levels 4-6, so the arm probably turned some level-sum wins into losses.

(4) The dose response fits a pure healing-loss cost: sp3 19-22 (p=0.76), sp5 18-17 (p=1.0), sp7 12-30 (p=0.008).

(5) A minor flaw: idx%10 < 3 makes all three flag defenders (idx 0-2) specialists. They rarely fight and stop healing at the flags.

(6) Correction: TACTICS.md says deaths "reset" attack XP. They do not; they cost 5-12 XP from the duck's highest skill, which delays mastery rather than resetting it.

(7) Weak evidence base. The source bot, jonters.bling3, loses to g_iter1 31 of 32 times in the census (86% in the survey). The one bot that beats us and was checked with --levels (kuma) shows the same heal-first cap we have. No bot that beats us is known to use T11; it came from reading the engine, not from copying a winning opponent.

Conclusion: the result shows that removing healing is costly. It does not show that attack mastery is worthless. Even a correct, XP-gated version can only pay in games that pass about r1100-1400, and our main loss mode (flags lost early, from below-par C10/C11) cuts those games off.
buildOrder: NEW:XP / skill-level steering and its measurement. Build: heal while healExp < 99, hold the 100th heal until attack reaches level 4, then heal freely; exclude defenders. Add to the census, per side, the level distribution at r1000/r1400/r2000 and end-of-game level sum. This step is cheap and should cost no healing and no level sum, so it is the only valid way to retest T11. Pre-register on games that pass r1200: attack level 4+ ducks per game, and level sum no lower than control.

C10 flag defence response: cut enemy pickups (17 vs 4) and losses before r1000 (46% of losses to the top 15), so games reach the window where mastery pays. This is worth doing whether or not T11 is retried.
C11 territory and tempo: get into the enemy half sooner (10 vs 24 robots at r250) for more contact, hence faster attack XP and kill crumbs.
C6 survival: fewer deaths per duck (5.2-5.8 against the top 15) means less XP lost to the jail penalty and fewer rounds without hits.
C4 kill-breakpoint targeting: prefer one-hit kills using rc.getAttackDamage, so the level-4 step (5 to 4 hits per kill after the ATTACK upgrade) turns into kills.

decompositions.name: Flank raid: a separate column takes a lightly held flag while the main armies are locked in an even fight

prerequisites.why: The tactic is a second group with its own target, its own route and its own launch moment, and it keeps going while the main fight continues.
prerequisites.evidence: Code: the squad is just ducks with index 3 to 12 (Duck.isRusher). They do the same setup() as the army, so they gather at the same dam. They leave at r201 with no launch trigger. When they respawn they head for the army's target (trySpawn uses fieldTargetFrom for every non-defender), not the squad's. Tests of different squad sizes never beat the control: arch_rush10 84/110 = control 84/110; vs g_iter1 arch_rush10 17/32, arch_rush20 12/32, all-out rush 5/32; fl6 7-11 (one seed); fl10 20-23 (two seeds). Census has no metric for this ('replay boards').

prerequisites.why: 'Locked in' means our main army holds the enemy army somewhere away from the target flag. Without that hold the target flag is not lightly held, and the army that lost 10 ducks gets pushed back.
prerequisites.evidence: Robots in the enemy half at r250 vs the 15 bots that beat us: 10 vs 24. In the 118 even-fight games (kill ratio 0.8-1.25): 11 vs 26. Our pickups grow with this metric: 1.0 per game when 0-5 of ours are in the enemy half, 4 at 6-10, 7 at 18+ (corr 0.29). Their pickups do not depend on their own count (corr -0.10; still 19 pickups when only 0-10 of theirs are in our half).

prerequisites.why: Choosing a lightly held flag needs to know where the enemy army and its defenders are, not just where the flags are. The flag positions themselves are nearly free.
prerequisites.evidence: First enemy-flag sighting r271 vs r232 vs beaters; r258 vs r233 in even-fight games. Broadcast hints give every dropped enemy flag to within dist2 100 from round 1, so finding the target is not the bottleneck. Nothing records where the enemy army is or how many guard each flag: missing.

prerequisites.why: The launch trigger, the choice of target and the route all need shared state: enemy army position, enemy count at each flag, and the squad's agreed target.
prerequisites.evidence: Code inspection of Comms.java: only slots 0-22 of 64 are used. There are no slots for enemy army position, defenders per flag, or squad target. Each rusher works out flankTarget() on its own from a mix of exact flag locations (EF_LOC) and noisy broadcast hints.

prerequisites.why: A flag taken on the far flank is carried a long way home with no main army nearby. The carrier has to survive the trip.
prerequisites.evidence: Carrier deaths per pickup, pooled over 444 games vs beaters: ours 0.87 vs theirs 0.66; in our losses 0.90 vs 0.64. Our carriers walk 11.7 moves (24.5 rounds) per pickup vs their 5.7 (17.7). carryFlag() takes a straight bug-nav line to the nearest spawn tile and does not route around enemies.

prerequisites.why: The raid pays only through pickups that turn into captures, and the relay is part of the arm.
prerequisites.evidence: Volume is below par: 5.5 vs 21.8 pickups per game pooled (medians 4 vs 17). The rate is at par: captures per pickup 0.115 vs 0.106, carrier speed 0.47 vs 0.45. The relay alone was neutral (a2relay 81/110 vs 84). The fl10 diagnostic had 84 pickups but only 3 captures (0.036 per pickup); relay hand-offs inflate the pickup count.

prerequisites.why: The main army has to keep the centre fight even with about 21% fewer bodies (47 to 37 field ducks).
prerequisites.evidence: Median per-game kill ratio vs beaters is 1.11 (us/them). We out-kill them by more than 25% in 42% of games, yet win only 32% of those, and they still pick up 17 of our flags per game in them. Guess: by Lanchester's square law, 37 vs 47 bodies is about (37/47)^2 = 0.62 of the fighting strength.

prerequisites.why: A flank column has to go around the centre fight, not straight through it.
prerequisites.evidence: No navigation stats in the census. Code: Nav.moveTo is greedy bug-nav with no lane or danger map. When rushers see enemies they call Micro.fight(goal), which uses RUSH_THREAT_COST 150 instead of the kiting value 1000, so they engage everything on the way.

prerequisites.why: Combat stun traps let a smaller army hold the centre. The opponent's own stun traps also defend its flag area against our raiders.
prerequisites.evidence: Traps built 187.5 vs 239; traps triggered 149.5 vs 221. Removing combat stun traps lost 16-26 in the ablation, the only trap habit that matters, and rushers never place them. CyrilSharma has 139 stun traps by r400 vs our 73.

prerequisites.why: A crumb bank pays for traps on demand, which defend without bodies and so free ducks for a detachment.
prerequisites.evidence: Crumbs gathered by r400 3900 vs 4950. Bank at r250 is about 240 for us vs 1000-6650 for the 11 banking bots that beat us. CyrilSharma: 4158 vs our 275.

prerequisites.why: Sending 10 ducks away must not weaken our home defence. Rushers skip alerts and carrier chases.
prerequisites.evidence: Enemy carriers killed per game: 11 vs 3. Per pickup it is less favourable: we kill 66% of their carriers, they kill 87% of ours. rush() returns before the alert, chase and combat-trap branches.

prerequisites.why: Squad ducks that die must come back to the squad, or the column fades.
prerequisites.evidence: Mean alive 44.9 vs 44.6, but code has a gap here: a respawned rusher spawns toward the army's target, not the flank target.

prerequisites.why: Enemy flags are often guarded by invisible stun traps paid for from a bank, not by bodies. A column that cannot infer where they are gets frozen (cooldown 40) at the flag.
prerequisites.evidence: Their traps are triggered 221 times per game vs our 149.5. Nothing in the code infers trap locations from stuns or from where the enemy spent crumbs. Guess-level importance.

prerequisites.why: Placing the squad on the flank during setup gives it a separate approach line from round 201.
prerequisites.evidence: Code: rushers run the shared setup() and gather at the dam with the army. No measurement.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
Two things went wrong at once: the test was inadequate, and the tactic's prerequisites are below par.

(1) The arm did not test T12 as observed. fl6/fl10/fl15 are arch_rush10 with one change, RUSH_FLANK (diffs of src/fl*/C.java). arch_rush10 had already scored exactly the control (84/110). The parts that define T12 were left out:
