- **No launch condition.** Nothing waits until the armies are locked. The squad does the shared setup(), gathers at the same dam, and leaves at r201.
- **No 'lightly held' choice.** flankTarget() picks the candidate farthest from the flag nearest our spawn centroid, purely by geometry, mixing exact locations with ±10 broadcast hints. A guess: this probably also picks the longest carry home.
- **No separate column.** Straight bug-nav plus Micro.fight(goal) means the squad engages everything on its way, in the open.
- **Respawns go to the army.** Dead rushers respawn toward the army's target.
- **Our strengths are lost.** The 10 rushers stop placing combat stun traps (load-bearing, ablation 16-26) and stop answering alerts and carrier chases (our C10).

(2) The readout cannot tell which mechanism failed. Band games gave only win/loss: 43 discordant pairs out of 240, net -3. The sign-test SE is about 6.6, so effects up to about ±4% win rate are invisible. fl6 has one seed and fl15 has none. The diagnostic was against g_iter1 (no banked trap defence, three lone defenders) and is not representative; even there 84 pickups gave only 3 captures. No capability census was run on the arm's band replays, so we cannot see whether the squad failed to convert or whether home and centre gave up as much as it gained. The comparator was g_iter1, not arch_rush10, so the flank target choice was never isolated.

(3) Prerequisites:
- **C1/C7 missing.** No shared picture of where the enemy army and its defenders are, so neither the launch trigger nor 'lightly held' can be computed.
- **C11 below par.** 10 vs 24 robots in the enemy half at r250; 11 vs 26 in even fights. Our army does not pin theirs, and our pickups track this metric (1 to 7 per game).
- **C9 below par.** 0.87 vs 0.66 carrier deaths per pickup, and our carries are about twice as long. A far-flank flag mostly dies on the way home.
- **C3/C5 below par.** Bank about 240 vs 1000-6650; traps triggered 149.5 vs 221. Their flags are defended by traps bought on demand, and our main army cannot hold with 21% fewer bodies (rush20 was worse than rush10, and all-out rush 5/32).

The census shows the opponent's flag-taking is decoupled from the fight. In games where we out-kill beaters by more than 25%, they still pick up 17 of our flags and capture about 2 per game. That decoupling is built on standing trap defence and forward territory that we lack. Copying only the detachment takes bodies from a main army that has no surplus to give.
buildOrder: Measurement first, not a capability: run the capability census on the existing fl10 and fl6 band replays and compare game by game with g_iter1 (our pickups and captures, their pickups, enemy carriers killed, carrier deaths per pickup). This says whether the squad failed to convert or home and centre collapsed; re-test the flank target against arch_rush10, not g_iter1.

C1 + C7: a shared picture of enemy disposition in the comms array (enemy army position and enemy count near each enemy flag, fed by sightings). It drives the launch trigger, the 'lightly held' target choice and route avoidance, and doubles as the flank early warning proposed as the T12 neutralization.

C9 (with C8): carrier survival on long carries (carrier routes away from visible enemies, escorts keep a formation around it, relay only to escorted allies). Target: 0.66 carrier deaths per pickup or better, from 0.87 now. Pays on every pickup, with or without a flank.
C3 then C5: bank crumbs through the fight and spend them on combat stun traps, so a smaller main army and lone flag defenders hold without bodies.
C11: the main army holds forward ground vs the bots that beat us (robots in the enemy half at r250 from 10 to 18 or more), which pins their army away from the raid target.

C12 (with C2, C6, C13): only then the conditional detachment. Launch when our army is engaged and the enemy army is known to be away from the target; pick the least-defended flag; route around the fight with a trap-aware danger map; respawn toward the squad; stage it during setup; keep rushers placing combat traps and answering nearby home alerts.

decompositions.name: Water traps (dig a radius-3 moat under an attacker's feet)

prerequisites.capability: NEW:usage-context trace (where and when the strong bots build their water traps)
prerequisites.why: The survey label merges two different uses. Strong bots place a small, fixed number of water traps each game. Weak bots place many as general combat traps. Until we know which use the strong bots make (flag moat, carrier moat or combat moat), we cannot know which capabilities a copy needs.
prerequisites.evidence: T7 was never traced (T10 and T12 were). The survey records only water400. Water traps per game for the bots that beat us: uravt exactly 3 in 28/28 games; andli28 2-5 (mode 3); hsmalladi 2-9 (mode 3); quesswho 3-9 (mode 3); Gymhgy 1-3; Strequals 0-3. For Gymhgy, water400 equals traps200 in 28/28 games, which suggests all of its water traps are built in setup. The heavy users place 13-35 per game and we beat them 71-100% of the time (dmtrung14 34.5, dylanzemlin 24, noahzemlin 18.5, tlevietpdx 18, AlexYu84 13). Across 55 opponents, the correlation between an opponent's water-trap count and its win rate against us is -0.05; for stun traps it is +0.75. In ONSET.md the us-minus-them water-trap correlation with winning is -0.04 to -0.08, inside the 0.19 noise floor. A fixed 3 per game matches the number of flags, so the strong use is probably anchored to flags (a guess).

prerequisites.why: A water trap fires on the same trigger as a stun trap (an enemy entering within dist2 2), so it pays only if it is placed where the enemy will step. Our copy reuses the combat-stun placement code (Duck.placeCombatTrap, line 474).
prerequisites.evidence: Against the 15 bots that beat us: trapsBuilt 187.5 vs 239, trapsHit 149.5 vs 221, hit rate 0.86 vs 0.92. Against the five water users alone we are at par (built 170 vs 159, hit 138 vs 138). Combat stun is our only trap habit that carries weight (ablation ab4nocombat 16-26). The dam, ring and float traps ablate to about zero (20-16, 20-19, 19-20).

prerequisites.why: A water trap costs 100 crumbs, the same as a stun, and uses the same action. Without a bank, a water trap can only replace the stun, never come on top of it. In t7water it replaced the stun.
prerequisites.evidence: Crumbs gathered by r400: 3900 vs 4950 against the bots that beat us. Bank at r250: ours about 240; the water users that beat us 950 (quesswho), 1288 (hsmalladi), 4158 (andli28), 6650 (uravt); SampleProvider 205. A combat trap needs at least 300 crumbs (100 plus TRAP_RESERVE 200).

prerequisites.why: A moat also blocks our own ducks. Nav.fillToward fills any water blocking a greedy step before falling back to wall-following (FILL_RESERVE 0). Each fill costs 30 crumbs and 30 action cooldown, so our ducks may spend crumbs and attack or heal turns undoing our own moat.
prerequisites.evidence: No navigation stats or fill counts were recorded for t7water. The census does not measure navigation. Code: src/bot/Nav.java lines 44 and 63-73.

prerequisites.why: The moat removes movement on both sides; robots on islands can still attack within dist2 4. It pays only if our micro uses the islands (hit from outside the moat, avoid being stranded while outnumbered). Our retreat and kiting, which matter most when outnumbered, are exactly what the moat takes away.
prerequisites.evidence: Raw fighting is even: kills 246 vs 292 overall against the top 15, 212 vs 220 in our losses, 267.5 vs 184 against the five water users. But Micro.fight looks only at canMove (Micro.java line 138) and has no term for water or escape routes, so it is blind to moats.

prerequisites.why: Likely the high-value use (a guess): a carrier can take no action except moving, so it cannot fill water. A moat near a flag strands a raider who has grabbed it until its allies fill a tile, which turns a fast defensive response into kills. This would also make T7 partly a neutralization of T1.
prerequisites.evidence: We kill carriers well: enemyCarrierKills 11 vs 3, and 20 vs 5 against the water users. We stop raids badly: they pick up our flags 17 times a game to our 4 (27 vs 6.5 against the water users) and capture 3 vs 0 in our losses. The flag-tile stun (n1flagstun) was rejected at 19-23.

prerequisites.why: The engine never digs spawn-zone tiles (GameWorld.triggerTrap line 409). Around a flag left at its spawn centre, a water trap only digs a ring at Chebyshev distance 2-3. A flag moved off the spawn zone gets a full moat. Four of the six bots that place a steady 2-4 water traps also move their flags in setup.
prerequisites.evidence: Our flagMoveDist is 0. Theirs: uravt 21, Gymhgy 13, hsmalladi 39, quesswho 17; andli28 and Strequals 0. Our T2 copy (a2reloc) scored 81/110 vs control 84 (neutral). Our setup traps (29 by r200) are worth about zero in the ablations.

prerequisites.why: The t7water trigger (outnumbered, at least 3 enemies in view) mostly fires when we are being pushed back. A moat there patches a symptom of low army presence forward rather than adding value.
prerequisites.evidence: Robots in the enemy half at r250: 10 vs 24 against the bots that beat us; 18 vs 13 in our wins.

prerequisites.why: A moat on a carrier's path, or at a flag being raided, needs fresh shared sightings of carriers and raiders.
prerequisites.evidence: Shared carrier sightings with chase and intercept were accepted in g_iter1 (+246 Elo; losses before r600 fell from 26 to 6). Shared-array schema in Comms.java.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation: Mostly the test was inadequate; missing capabilities explain only part of it. (1) It copied the wrong use. t7water is g_iter1 with WATER_WHEN_WEAK=true (src/t7water/C.java). When at least 3 enemies are in view, allies+1 < enemies and we hold at least 300 crumbs, the combat trap becomes a water trap (Duck.java:474). That is the volume, combat-moat style of the bots we beat. dmtrung14, noahzemlin, dylanzemlin, AlexYu84 and tlevietpdx build 13-35 water traps by r400, and we beat them 71-100% of the time. The bots that beat us build a small, fixed number: uravt exactly 3 in 28/28 games; andli28, hsmalladi and quesswho mode 3; Gymhgy 1-3, apparently all in setup; Strequals 0-3. That is only 3-9% of their traps (andli28: 91 water vs 1734 stun over 28 games). Water-trap volume does not track strength: correlation -0.05 across 55 opponents, against +0.75 for stun; the ONSET correlation is -0.04 to -0.08, inside noise. The fixed 3 matches the 3 flags, so the strong use is probably anchored to flags or carriers (a guess, not traced). Our arm tested something the top bots very likely do not do. (2) It was a substitution, not an addition. It replaced combat stun, our one trap habit that carries weight (ablation 16-26), in exactly the outnumbered fights where a stun's 40-cooldown freeze helps most. It also removes our own retreat (the moat surrounds our duck too) and may make our ducks spend crumbs and actions refilling it (Nav.fillToward). (3) The dose was never measured. The wt counter exists in the indicator string (G.java:40), but no diagnostic was logged. With our bank at about 240 at r250 and a 300-crumb floor, the trigger may be rare (a guess). (4) The block was underpowered. Over 4 band seeds we won 175/480 vs 165/480, 43-33 discordant (two-sided sign test p about 0.30; 49-38 with the field block, about 0.28). At that ratio, p < 0.10 needs about 155 discordant pairs, roughly 1000 band games. A 3-traps-a-game habit is plausibly worth a few games per 240, below the instrument's resolution of about 5 games. The capabilities that would also cap a correct copy: C3 bank (water can only replace the stun), C2 and C4 blind to water, and C10 raid prevention (17 vs 4 pickups).
buildOrder: NEW:usage-context trace: a replay-reader report of each water trap's build round and position relative to the builder's own flags, spawn zones and enemy carriers. Run it on kept replays of uravt (always 3), Gymhgy (setup only), andli28, hsmalladi and quesswho, to decide whether the strong use is a flag moat, a carrier moat or a combat moat

C10: a flag-defence response that converges on a stranded raider or carrier (stop raids, not only kill carriers: 17 vs 4 pickups). A flag or carrier moat amplifies exactly this, and it would also attack T1
C3: build a crumb bank (gathered400 3900 vs 4950; bank at r250 about 240) so a water trap is added on top of the combat stun that carries weight, not substituted for it
C2: water-aware navigation (do not reflexively fill our own moat in Nav.fillToward; route around it unless trapped) and record fills in the diagnostic
C4: micro that sees moats (an escape or island term; hit from outside the moat). Needed only if the trace shows combat use
C13: flag placement off spawn tiles (spawn tiles are never dug, so a moat around a spawn-held flag is only a ring). This links T7 to T2; helpful, not required

Retry as an additive arm (for example one water trap per home flag, or on an enemy carrier's path when the trace supports it). Run a diagnostic first that counts wt, fires, our fills and stranded carriers, then gate on about 1000 band games or stack it with another change

decompositions.name: Sustain fighting (heal-heavy): heal actions exceed attack actions by r400

prerequisites.why: The heal part of unit micro: heal targeting (lowest-HP ally within dist2 4), heal volume and heal skill levels. This is the only part of the surveyed symptom that is a behaviour rather than an outcome.
prerequisites.evidence: progress/survey.csv, 448 games vs the 16 that beat us: our median heal400 is 1160 vs their 948. We heal more than we attack in 93% of those games; they do in 62%. Median heal/attack ratio is higher for us than for the opponent against 14 of the 16 (only Gymhgy 1.70 and SampleProvider 2.54 are heavier than us). g_iter1 alone: 890 attacks and 1223 heals vs their 932 and 894, heal>atk in 97% of games. --levels: about 40 of 50 ducks reach heal mastery in long games. Fewer healers loses: sp7 (70% never heal) went 12-30.

prerequisites.why: The attack part of unit micro. Healing only pays if the healed unit turns back into damage. A heal is 80 HP for 30 cooldown; an attack is 150 damage for 20 cooldown. Every action spent healing instead of hitting is roughly a third of the damage.
prerequisites.evidence: Vs the 16: our median atk400 is 868 vs their 912, and 862 vs 927 in our losses. We take more total actions than they do (2049 vs 1857), so we are not idle; we are hitting less. Our win rate against them by attack difference at r400 (correlational): 0.00 at <= -300 (n=29), 0.05 at -300..-100, 0.14 at 0..100, 0.22 at 100..300, 0.50 at >= +300 (n=42). By our own heal/attack ratio: 0.38 at 0.9-1.1, 0.13 at 1.1-1.3, 0.05 at 1.3-1.5. The exchange itself is even: kills 224.5 vs deaths 225.5.

prerequisites.capability: NEW:heal rotation (hurt duck to healer, healer to hurt ally)
prerequisites.why: Deliberate sustain needs a hurt unit to go where it will be healed and healers to come to it. Without that, retreating only takes a unit out of the fight.
prerequisites.evidence: src/bot/Micro.java fight(): 'hurt' (HP < C.RETREAT_HP) only turns off the engage, advance and carrier-closing branches and adds -200 for standing within dist2 20 of an enemy. The only pull toward allies is +10 per ally within dist2 2, against -1000 per threat. tryHeal fires only with a hurt ally within dist2 4 and no enemy in reach. Healers never move toward hurt allies. Comms.java has no slot for hurt units or heal requests.

prerequisites.why: Rotating hurt units out and back in only helps if the army holds a front while they heal. Without a held line, a retreat gives up ground and tempo.
prerequisites.evidence: CAPABILITY_CENSUS, vs bots that beat us: inEnemy250 10 vs 24, inEnemy300 10 vs 22. In our wins it flips to 18 vs 13.

prerequisites.why: Stun traps freeze pursuers (cooldown 40), so a hurt duck can step out and be healed without being chased down.
prerequisites.evidence: Vs the 15 census bots that beat us: trapsHit 149.5 vs 221, trapsBuilt 187.5 vs 239. Ablation ab4nocombat lost 16-26 (combat stuns carry weight). Adding more combat traps was flat: ct1 20-22, ct2 16-18.

prerequisites.why: The crumbs that pay for the stuns covering a disengagement.
prerequisites.evidence: gathered400 3900 vs 4950 vs the bots that beat us. Survey bank at r250: ours ~240, theirs often 1000-6650.

prerequisites.why: Sustain is a substitute for respawning: a unit kept alive is worth the round trip from spawn plus the 25-round jail.
prerequisites.evidence: meanAlive 44.9 vs 44.6 vs the bots that beat us; 48.15 vs 38.2 vs the bots we beat.

prerequisites.capability: NEW:army cohesion (retreat and re-engage as a group)
prerequisites.why: Cross-year advice: 'retreat only near death, and as a group'. Rotating units requires a body that moves together.
prerequisites.evidence: No direct metric (C12 and cohesion are read only from replay boards). A forced regroup rule hurt in proportion to how hard it was enforced: gr4 20-23, gr8 4-18.

prerequisites.capability: NEW:skill-mix control (heal mastery caps attack at level 3)
prerequisites.why: Engine rule: once one skill reaches level 4, the others stop at level 3. A heal-heavy action mix makes most ducks heal masters and holds attack at level 3, so more sustain has a damage cost.
prerequisites.evidence: TRAINING_LOG iteration 10: about 40 of 50 g_iter1 ducks reach heal mastery first. jonters.bling3 has 20 attack masters; kuma shows the same cap as us. The specialisation arms (sp3/5/7) were rejected, so the right mix is still open.

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
Mainly the test was inadequate, for three reasons.

(1) The target was wrong: in the games that matter we already show this behaviour, and more strongly than the opponents. TACTICS/SURVEY mark 'we do it: no' from our median over all 1539 games (999 attacks, 805 heals). That median is dominated by 1091 games against bots we beat, where we attack 1095 and heal 637. In the 448 games against the 16 that beat us, we median 868 attacks and 1160 heals, with heals above attacks in 93% of games versus 62% for them. We are more heal-heavy than 14 of the 16. T6 says the same thing from the other side: top bots attack more and heal less than we do (975 vs 807, 1005 vs 1282). T6 and T8 read the same measurement, and adopting T8 pushes us further across the T6 gap. The symptom also does not tell bots apart: 32 of 55 opponents show it, 21 of them bots we beat 70-100% of the time.

(2) The knob did not implement sustain. In Micro.fight, C.RETREAT_HP only marks a duck 'hurt'. That turns off engage, advance and carrier-closing and makes it shy of enemies within dist2 20. Nothing moves a hurt duck toward a healer or a healer toward it (no comms slot, no positional pull beyond +10 per adjacent ally). So the dose ladder was really an aggression dose: more hurt ducks means fewer engagements and fewer attacks. Its shape matches that reading: 0:85, 150:83, 300:84, 500:82, 700:80, with the band at 17-19. The e1aggr and e2aggr arms showed the same flat response.

(3) There was no manipulation check. The t8hp arms have no per-game rows in survey.csv or the census, so nobody verified that heal/attack actually moved. And 110-game field blocks resolve only about ±5 games (log, 2026-10-01), so 80 to 85 is mostly noise.

The real prerequisites for a deliberate sustain doctrine are missing or below par: heal rotation (missing), a held front (C11: 10 vs 24 in the enemy half at r250), and stun cover (C5: 150 vs 221 trap hits). The heal behaviour itself is at par or better.

What the data points to instead (correlational) is attack conversion. Our win rate against these bots rises from 0.00 to 0.50 as our r400 attack margin goes from below -300 to above +300, and falls as our heal/attack ratio rises.

Guess, from code reading only and untested: the kite branch prefers holding at dist2 11-20 (+50). From that band no single step reaches attack range (dist2 <= 4). So a duck that becomes action-ready while holding there cannot take the engage branch, and its ready turns turn into heals. That would explain both our low attack count and our high heal count.
buildOrder: Fix the instrument first: score T6/T8 (and every 'we do it' flag) only on games against the 16 bots that beat us, not on all-games medians, and retire T8 as an adoption target. Add a per-arm counter for attacks and heals by r400 so each arm checks it moved the metric it targets (t8hp had no such check).

C4 attack conversion: raise attacks per r400 against the band from ~868 toward ≥ 930 without losing heal volume. First candidate (a guess to diagnose with a single game and the attacks/heals counters): a kite hold distance that lets a ready duck strike with one step, replacing the current dist2 11-20 band, or stepping in exactly on the turn the action cooldown clears.
C11 territory/tempo: hold a front in the enemy half (inEnemy250 10 -> ~20, the level seen in our wins). Without a held line, rotating units costs ground.
C5 combat stun cover funded by C3 (trapsHit 150 -> ~220; gathered400 3900 -> ~4900), so disengaging ducks are not chased down.

Only then the missing piece: heal rotation (a hurt duck moves toward the nearest healthy cluster or behind the front line, and healers with no enemy in reach step toward hurt allies), together with an attack/heal skill-mix rule so heal mastery does not cap attackers. Measure HP restored per heal and re-engagements per retreat before running a band block.

decompositions.name: Flag guards (6+ own robots within dist2 20 of own flags at r300)

prerequisites.why: Guard bodies come out of the field army. The guard bots that beat us can spare them because they still hold our half. We cannot: we already lose territory without spending extra bodies.
prerequisites.evidence: Census, games vs the bots that beat us: inEnemy250 is 10 (us) vs 24 (them) and inEnemy300 is 10 vs 22. In our wins it flips to 18 vs 13. Vs the 4 guard bots, their inEnemy250 is still 16/26/25/25 (NotLLeon/CyrilSharma/kyleezz/ColtG5) while ours is 13.5/12/2/3, even with 6-9 of their bodies near their flags. In 110 joined g_iter1 field games, our defend300 vs our inEnemy250 has r=-0.41: bodies near home mean we were pushed back.

prerequisites.why: A guard only beats a raid squad if it can spend at raid time, for example a stun under the raiders. Three of the four guard bots that beat us bank heavily. Our team bank at r250 is below even the combat-trap threshold.
prerequisites.evidence: Survey crumbs250: us 240; NotLLeon 5565, CyrilSharma 4158, kyleezz 1995, ColtG5 50. Census gathered400: 3900 vs 4950. placeCombatTrap (src/bot/Duck.java) needs at least 100+TRAP_RESERVE = 300 crumbs, so at our typical r250 bank a guard cannot trap at all.

prerequisites.why: Bodies only delay a rush; traps sprung by the raiders are what multiply a 2-guard post against a 10-duck squad. Our flag-side trap habits measure as worthless, and our combat-trap rule never fires against a small probe.
prerequisites.evidence: Census trapsBuilt 187.5 vs 239, trapHitRate 0.86 vs 0.92. Survey stun400: us 63; NotLLeon 94, CyrilSharma 139, kyleezz 65, ColtG5 58. Ablation ab2noring (no flag ring) 20-19, so the ring is worth about 0. Combat stun is load-bearing (ab4nocombat 16-26) but needs STUN_ENEMIES_MIN=3 visible enemies (C.java), so it never fires on a 1-2 duck probe of a flag.

prerequisites.why: Guards matter only as part of a raid-prevention loop: see raiders early, converge, deny the pickup. We kill carriers after the grab but do not prevent the grab, and every home-defence variant so far has lost.
prerequisites.evidence: Census vs the bots that beat us: they pick up our flags 17 times a game, we pick up theirs 4. Their captureRate is 0.13 vs our 0.06. enemyCarrierKills 11 vs 3: the reactive response works (g_iter1 chase gave +246 Elo) but prevention does not. Rejected home-defence arms: d1def2 9-25, d2alert 12-31, d3fort 16-29, flag-tile stun 20-25 (band 19-23).

prerequisites.capability: NEW:conditional role sizing (guards gated on army state / raid detection, relative to alive count)
prerequisites.why: The cross-year advice in research/ADVICE-crossyear.md (§12, §15) says a fixed one-guard-per-base strips the army where the threat is absent, and that defence should be sized relative to the army and gated on a measured trigger. Our defenders are fixed by creation index and never released to the field.
prerequisites.evidence: Duck.isDefender(): idx < 3*DEFENDERS_PER_FLAG, a constant. Defenders ring-walk their own flag; Duck.fieldTarget returns defendTarget() for them except during a carrier chase. There is no gate on alive count, territory or raid detection.

prerequisites.why: Guards fight outnumbered against raid squads and need good per-body exchange. This is not the binding gap.
prerequisites.evidence: Kills vs deaths in our losses: 212 vs 220. Vs all bots that beat us: 245.5 vs 292. Vs the 4 guard bots specifically we out-kill them 558 vs 323 (median), and they still beat us on flags.

prerequisites.why: Guards that die must re-enter at their flag. The guard bots keep their flags at spawn, so respawns there count as free guards.
prerequisites.evidence: meanAlive 44.9 (us) vs 44.6 (them). trySpawn already spawns defenders at their home flag and the army at the zone nearest the field target.

prerequisites.why: Guards act as sensors. An alert that carries raider count and direction could size the response. The naive version (wider alert radius) hurt.
prerequisites.evidence: From code inspection, Comms has only OF_ALERT (the round of the latest sighting per flag) and OF_CARRY: no count or direction. d2alert (radius dist2 100 -> 400) was rejected at 12-31.

prerequisites.why: Running a standing detachment beside a functional army is a form of force division.
prerequisites.evidence: No direct metric. Related arms were neutral: arch_rush10 squad 84/110 = control; fl10 flank squad 20-23 on the band.

prerequisites.why: Defensible flag spots would make guards cheaper. It is not needed to copy the bots that beat us: all four guard bots keep their flags at spawn.
prerequisites.evidence: Survey flagMoveDist is 0 for NotLLeon, CyrilSharma, kyleezz and ColtG5, the same as ours. Our relocation arm a2reloc was neutral (81/110 field, 20-21 vs arch_rush10).

decompositions.adoptionFailureExplanation:
Short answer: guards are trivial to build but only pay off on top of four capabilities where we are below par, so the 9-25 loss is what the prerequisites predict. The test also copied the measured number, not the opponents' traced mechanism, and the evidence says the number is mostly a symptom of losing ground.

**1. What we built.** d1def2 (TRAINING_LOG.md line 116) set C.DEFENDERS_PER_FLAG from 1 to 2. That gave 6 passive defenders instead of 3, each walking the 8 tiles around its spawn-held flag and building ring traps (Duck.defend). On the survey metric this takes us from about 5 to about 8, so the dose matched the guard bots that beat us (NotLLeon 9, ColtG5 8, CyrilSharma 6, kyleezz 6).

**2. Why it lost (paired mirror vs arch_rush10, 80 pairs, built before the trap-placement contamination, so the result is valid).**
- **The bodies cost territory we don't have.** Three more bodies (12% of the army) left a field army that already loses the territory battle (inEnemy250 10 vs 24 against the bots that beat us).
- **The guards had nothing to spend.** The team bank at r250 is about 240, but a combat stun needs at least 300 crumbs and at least 3 visible enemies. Ring traps are worth about 0 (ab2noring 20-19).
- **They were outnumbered.** Two guards facing a 10-duck squad are outnumbered about 5:1. Bodies only delay a rush.

The same pattern rejected every other home-defence arm: d2alert 12-31, d3fort 16-29, flag-tile stun 20-25 (band 19-23).

**3. Was the test adequate?**
- **For the narrow claim, yes.** "Unconditional standing guards bolted onto g_iter1 lose." The rush partner is the most favourable opponent guards could have and they still lost.
- **As a test of the tactic, no:**
  - It ran only as a mirror against our own partner, never on the rating band.
  - We never traced what the opponents' 6-9 near-flag bodies actually do. They could be fixed guards, fresh respawns (all four guard bots keep their flags at spawn), or healers.
  - It copied a small piece of a doctrine onto an unchanged strategy, which the cross-year advice (§12) warns cannot price that doctrine.
  - It had no relative sizing and no trigger.

**4. The bigger point: the survey feature looks mostly like a symptom, not a winning tactic.** defend300 counts the living robots within dist2 20 of each of a team's own uncarried flags at r300 (ReplayDump.java:361-372), so it mixes guard policy with "the fight is at my home".
- 26 of 39 bots we beat show it, against 4 of 16 that beat us.
- Across 55 opponents, Spearman between an opponent's median defend300 and our win rate against it is +0.40: the more they guard, the more we win.
- The 11 bots we beat at most 7% of the time have a median defend300 of 4, the same as ours (4-5).
- In 110 joined g_iter1 field games the losing side has the higher count. Ours is 4 in our wins and 12.5 in our losses; theirs is 9 in our wins and 4 in our losses.
- Within each of the 16 opponents that beat us: in games where their count is high, our win rate is 0.17 vs 0.09. In games where ours is high, their pickups are 18 vs 14 (median) and our win rate is 0.11 vs 0.18.
- Against the 4 guard bots we do no worse on flags than against the 11 non-guard bots that beat us. Pickups per game are 5.1 vs 5.7, captures per game 0.76 vs 0.58, pooled capture rate 0.147 vs 0.103, and our win rate 0.29 vs 0.10.

Their guards do not stop our raids better. What beats us is the rest of their package: territory, bank plus stun-heavy fighting (T5), and fast raids.

This last point is my reading of correlational data, not a controlled test. I have not traced the mechanism in any replay.
buildOrder: Step 0 (measurement, cheap and decisive): trace NotLLeon.v3 and CyrilSharma.finalBot at r250-r350 and classify their near-flag bodies as fixed guards, fresh respawns or healers. If they are mostly respawns or healers, drop T9 as a target.

C11 territory/tempo: raise robots in the enemy half at r250 from 10 toward 18 or more vs the bots that beat us. This is the metric that flips in our wins, and it is what lets a team spare guard bodies.
C3 crumb economy and bank: hold 1000 or more crumbs through r250-r400 (now about 240; gathered400 3900 vs 4950), so a guard can afford a stun when raiders arrive.

C5 combat-trap conversion at the flag: let a duck at its home flag place a stun from 1-2 visible raiders when the bank allows. The current rule needs 3 or more enemies and 300 or more crumbs. Measure trap hits by raiders within dist2 20 of our flags.
C10 prevention, not only carrier kills: push enemy pickups per game down from 17. Add a metric for the rounds from the first raider seen within dist2 36 of a flag to its first pickup.
NEW conditional role sizing: release guards to the field unless a raid is detected or the army is ahead (alive count, inEnemy), and size the guard count to the alive count.
Then retry T9 as 1 guard per flag plus a bank-funded stun plus a second guard only on a raid trigger. Judge it on the band (2 seeds, 240 games) as well as vs arch_rush10, never on the mirror alone.

methods.angle: STRUCTURAL / DESIGN: a prerequisite dependency graph (PDG). Its edges come only from engine rules (RULES.md) and code paths in src/bot. Each capability node is marked par or below par from the census (paired, per game, against the 15 bots that beat us). A tactic's label is the number of below-par ROOT capabilities, plus other tactics, on the path from its actions to a win term. One extra rule separates root deficits from inherited ones: a downstream deficit that disappears in the games where its graph parents are at par is inherited, and is not counted again.
methods.method:
PDG METHOD (mechanical).
STEP 1 NODES. P = engine primitives: move, fill, attack, heal, build{stun, water, explosive}, dig, pickup/drop, spawn, sense (vision dist2 20 + broadcast hints), shared array, buyGlobal.
C = capabilities C1..C14 (research/CAPABILITIES.md), split where the census measures parts separately:
- C3a gathering, C3b banking/pacing, C3c kill-reward income (new)
- C5v trap volume, C5p trap placement/hit rate
- C8c carriage/conversion, C8v pickup volume
- C10k carrier kills, C10p pickup prevention
New nodes:
- C15 global-upgrade timing
- C16 flag-zone presence (bodies around a contested flag inside the 4-round return window; proposed, unmeasured)
T = tactics.

STEP 2 EDGES (u->v means v needs u). Only engine-rule or code-path edges are allowed:
- C11->C1: vision dist2 20, so sighting needs presence; broadcast is only +-10 tiles.
- C11,C2->C3a: crumbs are collected only by stepping on the tile.
- C11->C3c: +30 crumbs per kill only when the attacker stands on enemy territory.
- C3a,C3b,C3c->C5v: traps cost 100/200.
- C4,C11->C9: a carrier cannot act and has +20 move cooldown.
- C2,C9->C8c.
- C1,C11,C4->C8v: pickup needs dist2 2.
- C7,C6,C4,C5p->C10k/C10p: alerts; respawn only in own spawn zones.
- C2,C4,C6->C11: jail lasts 25 rounds; respawn is at home.
- C7,C11->C12: the main front must hold with fewer bodies.
- C4(survival)->C14: jail resets the highest skill's XP.
- C3b->setup dig budget.
- C16->C8v,C10p,C9: a dropped flag can be picked up again next round and returns home after 4 rounds.

STEP 3 PER TACTIC.
- Target(t) = capabilities its own arm counters move directly.
- E(t) = capabilities its actions use.
- Pay(t) = capabilities on the engine path from its direct effect to a win term (CAPTURE / MORE_FLAG_CAPTURES / LEVEL_SUM).
- Prereq(t) = (E union Pay) minus Target. Two additions: (a) if a Target capability is INHERITED, its roots join Prereq, because the tactic cannot produce a symptom without its cause; (b) a requirement above every beater's observed level counts as BELOW.
- K(t) = tactics whose output state t needs (for example, carriers for a relay).

STEP 4 STATUS, over the 444 paired games vs the 15 beaters. d = oriented (us - them); timings are counted from r200. P = share of games with d >= 0; R = oriented ratio of medians.
- BELOW iff P < 0.40 AND R < 0.85.
- ABOVE iff P > 0.60 and R > 1.15.
- UNMEASURED if there is no metric.
- PAR otherwise.

STEP 5 ROOT vs INHERITED. For a BELOW node, recompute P on the games where every measured parent has d >= 0. If P >= 0.40 it is INHERITED (its roots are its below-par parents); otherwise it is ROOT.

STEP 6. b(t) = the number of distinct ROOT below-par nodes in Prereq(t), each counted once.

STEP 7 LABEL.
- elementary: K empty and b = 0 (depth 1).
- intermediate: K empty and b = 1 (depth 2).
- composite: K non-empty or b >= 2 (depth >= 3).
- undetermined: the label flips depending on the status of an UNMEASURED prereq.

STEP 8 VALIDATE against TRAINING_LOG. Prediction: elementary arms move their counters and read their own value. Intermediate and composite arms move their counters but stay neutral until their roots are fixed.

STEP 9 COST. For each capability, cost = P(below) x the within-opponent (Mantel-Haenszel) difference in win rate between games at par and games below par, with a 90% bootstrap confidence interval. Inherited costs are reported under their root. Fixed-round metrics are preferred over whole-game ones, which are upper bounds because they move with the outcome. Experimental evidence (arms and ablations) overrides an association when the two disagree.

methods.limitations:
- The census is observational. The root/inherited test conditions on variables that move with the outcome. Within-opponent MH removes opponent strength but not map or game-length confounding. Whole-game metrics (traps built, pickups, carrier survival, capture rate) give upper-bound costs.
- Small conditioning sets: n = 43-104 for most tests, and only 13/17 beater games for the stun400 split.
- The thresholds (P < 0.40 and R < 0.85) are arbitrary, and two labels sit on a knife edge:
  - T1 depends on C9 at 17/43 = 0.395; at 0.40 it becomes intermediate.
  - T5 depends on C5v being inherited at P 0.41 (n = 59); if C5v were a root, T5 would be elementary.
- Drawing a tactic's boundary (Target vs Prereq) and its payoff path takes judgement. T4's label is specific to how it was implemented: the DIG_RESERVE gate made a below-par bank a prerequisite.
- Our pickups minus theirs is the same paired number as pickups allowed, so the census cannot separate our flag offence from our flag defence.
- Pickups mix first grabs, relays and re-grabs; there is no flag-excursion metric. C16 (flag-zone presence / re-grab) is a hypothesis built from the engine rule (re-pickup next round, return after 4 rounds) and the 11 carrier kills vs 17 pickups. It is not measured.
- C3c, C7, C12 and C16 are unmeasured. Engine edges give their direction but not their size.
- Arms have no census rows: survey.csv lacks territory and carrier metrics, so we cannot check whether e1aggr or fl10 moved C11 or C9.
- Validation is weak: almost every arm is neutral. The prediction that non-elementary tactics stay neutral until their roots are fixed (10 of 10 consistent) is hardly falsifiable. The elementary arms are T7 (lean positive, p ~ 0.24) and T8 (closed, already at par).
- Status is relative to the median of the 15 beaters in one incumbent's games on a fixed map mix, not to the top of the field.
- No replays were read (2 GB host), so mechanisms such as re-grabs and kill-reward income are not verified.
- Suggested next measurements (new replay-dump modes, to run elsewhere):
  - flag excursions and re-grabs within 4 rounds of a carrier death;
  - bodies within dist2 20 of contested flags;
  - kill-reward crumbs by territory;
  - territory and carrier metrics for the arms;
  - a c5bank + digging stack, which would test T4 fully for the first time.

methods.angle: Cross-opponent statistics over 55 opponents of different strength. A tactic counts as elementary if weak bots produce it about as often as strong bots, and if its link to winning does not depend on a bot's basic capabilities. A tactic counts as composite if only strong bots show it, it co-clusters with other strong-only tactics, and its link to winning disappears once basic-capability metrics are held fixed. In that case the tactic marks an infrastructure stack and is not a lever on its own. Headline result: across the 55 opponents, five basic-capability metrics predict opponent strength with leave-one-out R2 0.77. Adding all 11 tactic flags leaves it at 0.77. The tactic flags alone reach 0.51. Every bit of strength information the tactics carry is already in the capability metrics, mainly fight parity (C4/C5) plus territory and sighting (C11/C1). That supports the owner's hunch: work on the basics, not on copying tactics.
methods.method:
Scripts are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-terryvanbelle-projects-vibe-2024/0c12d742-3a89-49d0-8e9e-654c983bb00e/scratchpad: common.py, s1_prevalence.py, s2_cooccur.py, s3_condition.py, s4_within.py, s5b_capcost.py, s6_extra.py, s7_r2.py. They are pure python3 and read only the CSVs.

STEP 0 – Turn each tactic into a measurable test. Each tactic becomes a per-game test on the opponent's row in progress/survey.csv. An opponent "shows" the tactic if the test passes on its median over about 28 games, using the thresholds from tools/tactics-survey.py:
- T1: 0 < firstPickup <= 260
- T2: flagMoveDist >= 6
- T3: drops >= 3
- T4: digs200 >= 20
- T5 (full tactic): crumbs250 >= 1000 AND traps200 <= 6 AND stun400 >= 60. Its parts are scored separately as bank (crumbs250 >= 1000) and stun (stun400 >= 60).
- T6: atk400 >= 500 and atk400 > heal400
- T7: water400 >= 3
- T8: heal400 > atk400 > 0
- T9: defend300 >= 6
- T10 (full tactic): the bank grows by 1000+ crumbs between r200 and r250 in at least 25% of games, AND the bot is stun-heavy
- T12 (proxy): the opponent picks up our flags 10+ times while its kill share is 0.4–0.6, in at least 20% of games
- T11: no column measures it, so it is not tested.
A tactic that has several parts is labelled on all of its parts together, and each part is also reported.

STEP 1 – Prevalence by strength tier. Tiers come from our survey win rate against each opponent:
- S (strong): we win 50% or less (16 bots)
- M (middle): we win 50–90% (6 bots)
- W (weak): we win more than 90% (33 bots)
Compute pW (share of weak bots showing the tactic), pS, and a two-sided Fisher exact test of S against W.
- CHEAP: pW >= 0.15, i.e. at least 5 of the 33 weak bots show it.
- STACK-ONLY: pW < 0.10 AND Fisher p < 0.05 AND pS > pW.
- Anything else is GREY.

STEP 2 – Co-occurrence (used to corroborate, not to decide). Compute the phi matrix of the opponent-by-tactic flags, then cluster with average linkage on distance 1−phi. The "core" tactics are those with Fisher p < 0.05 and lift >= 2.5: T3, T4, stun, T10, T12. For each tactic, report how many other core tactics its bots show, and its coefficient on strength once the count of other core tactics is held fixed.

STEP 3 – Holding capabilities fixed (the deciding test).
- Strength = logit of the opponent's shrunk win share against us, (L+0.5)/(n+1).
- Regression: ordinary least squares across the 55 opponents. Compare three models: the tactic flag alone; the flag plus the early capability set; the flag plus the early+fight set.
  - Early set (all z-scored opponent medians of them-minus-us from the census): C11 = robots in the enemy half at r250, C1 = lead in first enemy-flag sighting, C3 = crumbs gathered by r400.
  - Early+fight set adds C4 = kill share from the survey, and C5 = trapsHit difference.
- Confidence intervals come from 1000 bootstrap resamples of opponents. Retention R = coefficient after conditioning ÷ raw coefficient.
- Results are corroborated two ways. First, a logistic regression over the 700 census games, weighted so each opponent counts equally, with standard errors clustered by opponent. Second, within-opponent Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios on the survey, stratified by opponent and then by opponent × kill-share tercile.
- Outcomes:
  - MARKER: the raw interval excludes 0, the early+fight conditioned interval includes 0, and R < 0.5.
  - RESIDUAL: the conditioned interval excludes 0.
  - NONE: the raw interval includes 0.

DECISION RULE
- undetermined: no feature measures the tactic, or fewer than 4 bots show it.
- elementary: CHEAP, and not a positive MARKER.
- composite: STACK-ONLY AND MARKER.
- intermediate: everything else. That means STACK-ONLY with a residual, GREY prevalence, or CHEAP but a positive marker.

READING THE LABELS
- elementary means a weak bot can build it. It says nothing about whether it helps; the reason for each tactic gives the value evidence.
- composite means the tactic's apparent value travels with the basic capabilities. Adopting it alone is predicted not to pay. That matches the neutral or negative adoption arms.

CAPABILITY-DEFICIT RANKING (s5b)
- For each census metric (us minus them), compute our mean deficit against the 15 bots that beat us, in SD units, with values capped at the 5th and 95th percentiles.
- Estimate how much each SD is worth with a within-opponent linear probability model: the win and the metric are both centred on the opponent's own mean, with bootstrap intervals by opponent. Then cost = −slope × deficit, i.e. the win points we would gain by reaching parity.
- Two extras:
  - The capture gap is decomposed into pickup volume versus capture per pickup.
  - Early (r400) versions from the survey (stun400, atk400, crumbs250, firstPickup) are checked for whether a deficit exists before the game is decided.

methods.limitations:
- **Elementary tells you cost to build, not value.** Prevalence among weak bots shows a behaviour pattern can be produced without a strong stack. Weak bots often produce it for a different reason: the banking in T5 and T10 comes from bots that never spend, not from deliberate saving. I partly handled this by labelling multi-part tactics on all their parts together. The opposite also happens: T4 (digging) is trivial to code but labelled composite, because the stack it marks is the author's sophistication, not code infrastructure.

- **Conditioning cannot tell a marker from a mechanism.** A link that vanishes once capabilities are held fixed may mean the tactic only marks a strong stack, or that the tactic is *how* the bot gets that capability. Stun traps winning fights is the obvious case. Either way the basic capability is the measurable target, but a composite label does not prove the tactic is useless.

- **The fight covariates are partly outcomes.** Kill share and trapsHit are whole-game counts, so conditioning on them may over-control. The early set (C11, C1, C3) is cleaner but weaker.

- **Small samples:**
  - Only 16 strong opponents.
  - Capability medians for 35 of the 55 opponents come from just 2 field games each. That noise under-adjusts, so retention figures are biased up.
  - Bootstrap intervals are wide.
  - 13 tactics × 3 models with no multiple-comparison correction.
  - Several cut-offs are arbitrary (pW 0.15 / 0.10; T7 sits exactly at 5 of 33).
  - T1's enrichment flips with the pickup-round threshold.

- **Strength means strength against us.** It is our win rate against each opponent, over 13 of our builds. Tactic features are measured in games against us, so they are partly reactions to how we play.

- **T11 and T12 lack a direct test.** T11 has no measure. T12 is an outcome-signature proxy (pickups at fight parity) that presupposes C4 parity by definition, so its composite label is partly built in.

- **Within-opponent tests are weak.** Setup tactics are fixed policies with no variation between games (T4: 1 informative opponent). Flag tactics executed in a game depend on the outcome: T3's drops require pickups, and T1's early pickups require an open defence.

- **The cost figures are not causal.** They come from within-opponent game-to-game variation. They are attenuated and assume that this slope carries over to closing a structural gap between opponents.

- **Every single-capability cost is small (≤4 points, except the outcome-adjacent ones).** Our win rate against these bots is 16%, so no single basic explains the gap. It is a bundle centred on territory and pickup volume.

- **Unmeasured capabilities:** C2, C7 and C12 have no direct metric here.

- **Weak validation against the adoption arms.** The method agrees with all ~25 neutral or negative arms (composite tactics predicted not to pay; T7, the one cheap tactic with a residual, is also the one arm that leaned positive). But every arm was flat, so the agreement cannot discriminate between methods.

methods.angle: Experimental protocol. A tactic counts as "elementary" if our own copy of it (a) fires, (b) by itself recreates the state the opponents show, and (c) does the same thing whatever base build or prerequisite it sits on. It needs infrastructure if the copy runs short of something else we lack (starved), if its effect appears only when a named prerequisite is switched on or the opponent is handicapped in that prerequisite, or if taking bodies or crumbs for it costs more as the dose rises. Before the new tests, I went through the existing log (about 25 arms since g_iter1) and recorded which of these tests had already been run in effect. The main finding is that several "neutral" verdicts were never verdicts on the tactic. The arm never recreated the opponents' state: setup digging had a median of 0 digs, banking moved our r250 bank by +97, and the aggression arms raised heals as much as attacks.
methods.method:
FIRE-REPRODUCE-CONVERT-DEPEND protocol (FRCD). Inputs per tactic T: an arm A_T (the smallest code change that does T); a mechanism counter m_T (indicator string); a proximate state metric s_T, which the census/survey reader measures for both teams (T1/T12 captured; T2 enemy firstPickup and pickups; T3 captured and carrierSpeed; T4 digs200 and level200; T5 crumbs250; T6/T8 atk400 vs heal400; T7 water400 and kills while outnumbered; T9 defend300 and enemy pickups; T10 gathered r200-400 and crumbs250; T11 attack masters via --levels); the opponents' census value s_opp and our control value s_ctl; and the named candidate prerequisites P_T (C-ids upstream of s_T in the census chain).
Step F (fire): one logged diagnostic game per base. PASS if m_T fires at >= 50% of the claimed rate. FAIL means the code is inert: fix it and assign no label.
Step R (reproduce): on the arm's own paired cells (240 band games, or 110 field cells), compute ds = mean(s_arm - s_ctl). Classify:
- PASS if ds >= 0.5*(s_opp - s_ctl).
- STARVED(k) if the mechanism ran short because k distinct resources or states of ours (bank, bodies, pickups or escorts, survival, centre presence) stayed below what it needs. The evidence is the arm's own counters or survey columns.
- COMPLETED-NO-EFFECT if the mechanism completed its action but s_T did not move for an engine or opponent reason.
- EMERGENT if s_T moves together with its opposite under the knob, or flips with game state in our own control games.
Step C (convert): paired gained-lost over 240 band games (2 seeds x 120, identical cells), sign test; resolution about +-5 games. This is reported as VALUE only, not as part of the label.
Step D (depend), run only after R=PASS:
(a) Transfer. The same patch on g_iter0 (judged on its own band) and on g_iter1. Effect e_b = gained - lost, SE_b = sqrt(gained + lost). Dependence if |e0 - e1| > 2*sqrt(SE0^2 + SE1^2).
(b) 2x2 interaction with one named prerequisite P toggled. Either P on/off in our build, or, cheaper, the opponent's P handicapped in a paired mirror: A_T vs g_iter1-with-P-degraded against A_T vs intact g_iter1. Dependence if the interaction exceeds 2 SE.
(c) Resource dose. If T takes bodies, crumbs or actions from the army, run a dose ladder of 3 or more points. A monotone negative step pattern means T needs a surplus of that resource.
DECISION RULE (label = dependency, not value):
- ELEMENTARY: F=PASS, R in {PASS, COMPLETED-NO-EFFECT}, and no dependence in D. If D has not been run: no negative resource dose, and T uses only capabilities that both g_iter0 and g_iter1 have.
- INTERMEDIATE: exactly one named prerequisite, found by STARVED(1), by one D dependence, or by a negative dose in one resource.
- COMPOSITE: STARVED(k>=2), EMERGENT, or two or more dependencies. Also composite if T fires and moves s_T but fails to convert to captures or wins while the opponents' version converts, and two or more census deficits sit on the chain.
- UNDETERMINED: F or R not measured and no D evidence.
A STARVED label is provisional: if the starving resource can be freed cheaply (shown by ablation), re-run the arm at the reproduced dose before closing it.
CAPABILITY RANKING RULE: Use only early metrics (<= r400) from the 444 census games vs the 15 bots that beat us. Rank by deficit cost = (share of games in deficit) x (Mantel-Haenszel win-rate difference between parity and deficit, stratified by opponent, with bootstrap 90% CI). Cross-check with a logistic model with opponent fixed effects ('close this one deficit' counterfactual). Report outcome-adjacent metrics (pickups, enemy pickups, carrier deaths, meanAlive) but rank them below the early ones because of reverse causation. Break ties by upstream position (correlation with other deficits). Ablation and upgrade-order results mark capabilities as load-bearing (protect) as opposed to in deficit (build).
TESTS ALREADY RUN IN EFFECT:
- Transfer to g_iter0: none for any tactic. Only the g_iter0 -> g_iter1 stack of basic repairs (C1 symmetry, C10 carrier chase, C11 advance, C3/C5 float spending), which transferred (mirror 27-1, field +246 Elo), the only accept in the log.
- Opponent-class transfer: arch_rush10 53% vs g_iter1 but field 84=84; fl10 and sp5 won their diagnostics vs g_iter1, band 20-23 and 18-17. These work against our own base, not against the band.
- Interaction cells: c5bank (bank alone) / ct2 (spend alone) / c6pair (bank + spend), but on mixed instruments and with the bank never reproduced. a2reloc 81 vs a2relay (= reloc + relay) 81: relay adds 0 given relocation. t7water x t8hp0 = s1stack 19-17: no interaction.
- One-factor knock-outs: ab1-ab4 (only combat stun traps are load-bearing, 16-26); up2 capturing-first 14-33 (ATTACK upgrade load-bearing).
- Dose ladders: T8 RETREAT_HP 0..700; T11 sp3/5/7; T12 fl6/10/15; gr4/8; T4 dig5/10; T6 e1/e2; ct1/ct2.
- Sparring vs arch_rush10: d1def2 9-25, d2alert 12-31, d3fort 16-29, a2reloc 20-21, n1flagstun 20-25.
- Step R had never been checked. I computed it now from survey.csv for the 11 field arms on paired cells; see perTactic.

methods.limitations:
1. The capability ranking is correlational. It uses 444 games of a single build (g_iter1). Even metrics taken by r250-r400 partly reflect how the r200-r250 fights went (reverse causation). Map effects are only partly cancelled by using us-minus-them differences. Opponent fixed effects control for opponent strength, not within-game confounds. The effects are modest: closing every early deficit at once predicts 16% -> 22% vs the beaters. That is about +7 games on a 240-game band block, near the instrument's ~5-game resolution. The territory story is weaker within strong opponents (MH CI touches 0; logistic CI includes 0) than the headline 18-vs-13 flip suggests.
2. Step R uses survey.csv. That file covers only the 11 field arms on 110 cells (30 vs the beaters, so cuts like a2reloc's +4.7 enemy pickups are noisy). The band arms (t7water, t8*, t10crumbs, sp*, fl*, ct*, ab*, gr*, up*) have no local per-game replays. For those, the labels rest on diagnostics, dose curves and log text, not on a measured reproduction.
3. The 50%-of-gap threshold for Step R and the 2-SE dependence bars are conventions, not derived. STARVED attributions read the arm's counters by hand, and a different reader could count the prerequisites differently (T3 and T11 are arguably 2).
4. A STARVED label describes our copy as much as the tactic. T4 and T5 may move to elementary or intermediate once the setup budget is freed and the arm is re-run at the opponents' dose.
5. The g_iter0 transfer test confounds every g_iter0 -> g_iter1 difference (C1 symmetry, C10 chase, C11 advance, float spending, setup traps). It detects dependence on that bundle, not on a named capability. g_iter0 also needs its own rating band, so effects must be compared on an Elo scale. Tactics added later as constants also need porting into g_iter0's code.
6. Interactions need roughly 2-4x the games of a main effect at the same resolution: a 2x2 is 4 blocks of 240. At the current +-5-game resolution, interactions below about 7-10 games are invisible.
7. A null effect on both bases does not prove a tactic elementary. It may depend on a capability that neither g_iter0 nor g_iter1 has; T12 likely needs a C11 superiority neither build has. The handicapped-mirror test only approximates boosting our own capability, is asymmetric, and is mirror-specific (ADVICE: the mirror is blind to weaknesses both builds share).
8. Sparring partners are self-derived: arch_rush10 is g_iter1 plus a squad, so it can co-adapt with us. Single diagnostic games (fl10, sp5, gr8) are filters, not evidence.
9. The census metrics have blind spots. trapsBuilt and kills are full-game totals that game length confounds (our wins vs the beaters run to r2000; losses median r1082). C2, C7 and C12 have no opponent metric. The proposed dam-break metric (kills and centre-crumb share r200-r260) does not exist yet.
10. The labels classify dependency, not value. 'Focus on basics' rests on two things: the correlational ranking, and the log's record that the only accept (g_iter1) was a stack of basic repairs while every copied tactic was neutral. Neither is a controlled test of a basics-first programme.

critiques:
1. **§3 block 3 (C3 crumb income after the dam), and the FRCD claim "our wins gather +1500 more in r200-r400 than our losses, for all 8 opponents tested"**
   - **What is wrong:** the r200-r400 gap separates wins from losses only because of the opponents' gathering. Our own gathering does not separate them.
   - **Evidence:** in the 444 beater games, our r200-r400 gathering has a median of 200 in wins vs 300 in losses (means 1364 vs 1285). Theirs is 250 vs 1050 (means 2027 vs 3415).
   - **Evidence:** per opponent, our own wins-minus-losses gathering is negative for 9 of 13 opponents (for example NotLLeon −1463, andli28 −1373, jmerle −1110). So "+1500 for all 8" is false for our gathering.
   - **Evidence:** gathering is reported in steps of 100 crumbs, so 174 of 444 games (39%) have a gap of exactly 0. The tercile win rates depend on how ties are split: 0.09/0.14/0.25 in the draft, 0.087/0.174/0.276 or 0.089/0.136/0.207 with value cuts, and 0.088/0.061/0.324 with a rank split.
   - **Fix:** split the gap into our part and their part. The proposed in-contact crumb sweep targets the part that does not separate wins from losses. Retarget the block to their income (kill bounty and centre control) or demote it. Drop "steepest early gradient".

2. **§3 block 5: "does not correlate with our pickups (rho −0.05)", and the sighting terciles**
   - **What is wrong:** this is a sentinel artefact.
   - **Evidence:** 18 beater games have `firstFlagSight = 0`, meaning we never saw a flag. All 18 have 0 pickups and all 18 are losses, yet they are ranked as the earliest sightings. Including them gives rho −0.046.
   - **Evidence:** excluding them gives rho −0.15 (n = 426, about 3 SE), and the sighting gap (us minus them) against our pickups gives −0.22.
   - **Fix:** treat 0 as missing or as censored at game end. Re-run the C1 tercile and correlation analysis, and the PDG status of C1.

3. **§1.1 pattern 2: "We already 'do' the fast part of T1: our median first pickup is r248"**
   - **What is wrong:** r248 is the median over all 1539 survey games: every build, every opponent, and including 119 zero sentinels (no pickup). This is the same "median over all games" error the draft criticises for T8.
   - **Evidence:** g_iter1 against the beaters is r362.5 (excluding 14 of 60 games with no pickup), against their r254-272. The T1 row of the draft itself uses r359.
   - **Fix:** remove the claim and drop the XO "elem" reading of T1.

4. **§3 block 7: "At r400 the per-game stun gap is only −4.6, so most of the gap opens after r400 and follows the result"**
   - **What is wrong:** in beater games the gap is already large by r400.
   - **Evidence:** g_iter1 against the 15 beaters (survey, 60 games): stun400 is 50.5 vs 72 (mean difference −16). Fight-phase traps over r200-r400 (stun + explosive + water by r400, minus setup traps) are 24 vs 72.5, three times fewer.
   - **Evidence:** the −4.6 is presumably a cross-opponent figure that includes weak bots we out-trap. The draft's own block 4 says "ours are 24-39, theirs 65-69".
   - **Fix:** C5 volume is an early deficit, not an inherited one. Re-derive the C5 status and its ranking.

5. **§3 block 2: "their captures do [separate wins from losses] (1.1 vs 2.5)", and "We beat them by keeping our flags long enough"**
   - **What is wrong:** this is the scoreboard. CAPTURE means three enemy captures and MORE_FLAG_CAPTURES means more enemy captures, and 249 + 112 = 361 of our 374 beater losses ended one of those two ways.
   - **Fix:** do not use enemy captures to rank conversion defence. Use pre-outcome quantities, such as the re-grab share once it is measured.

6. **"Protect: C10 carrier interception: 11 vs 3 a game"**
   - **What is wrong:** the count reflects exposure, not skill. They carry about 4 times as often (21.8 vs 5.5 pickups per game).
   - **Evidence:** per carrier we kill 0.66 of theirs; they kill 0.87 of ours. These are the draft's own block-6 numbers (carrier deaths per pickup).
   - **Evidence:** C10 is also marked − in the T1, T2, T9 and T11 rows. C6 has the same problem: "C6 routing −" in T2 but + in T11 and in the Protect list.
   - **Fix:** use per-opportunity rates and give each capability one status across the document.

7. **"Protect: C4 micro: kills 212 vs 220 in our losses", "fights even", and "no single basic is a large win lever inside the band"**
   - **What is wrong:** 212-220 is the figure over all 414 losses, 40 of which were to non-beaters. In the 374 beater losses it is 200 vs 258.
   - **Evidence:** within beater games, kill share has the steepest gradient: win rate by tercile 0.03 / 0.07 / 0.37. Its correlation with winning is rho 0.43, against 0.06 for territory, and its Mantel-Haenszel difference is +0.13 against +0.08.
   - **Evidence:** "beater games" are not the band. The band has 6 non-beaters, and uravt is not in it.
   - **Fix:** kill share is a whole-game metric and partly an outcome, but so is gathered400, which the draft promotes. Either both are suspect or both count. Do not generalise from territory to "no single basic".

   - **What is wrong:** under rule (a), most of §3's own metrics would be retired as symptoms.
   - **Evidence for rule (a):**
     - inEnemy250 flips: 19 v 11 against bots we beat, 10 v 24 against beaters; 18 v 13 in our wins, 11 v 24 in our losses.

   - **What is wrong:** these are pooled over the 110 field games, 80 of them against non-beaters. Within the 30 beater games, r = 0.18 and 0.16.
